title: Facets of Personality: Taking Control, Taking Chances, and Finding Happiness
overview: Instead of offering one grand theory of the whole person, this chapter examines three narrow, intensively researched facets of personality. Julian Rotter's locus of control describes whether people believe their reinforcements come from their own behaviour (internal) or from luck, fate and powerful others (external); it is measured with the I-E Scale and is linked to age, gender, culture, behaviour, mental and physical health, and parenting. Marvin Zuckerman's sensation seeking is a largely inherited need for varied, novel, complex and intense experience, measured with the Sensation Seeking Scale and made up of four components (thrill and adventure seeking, experience seeking, disinhibition, boredom susceptibility); it predicts risk taking, drug use, personality, cognition, job interests and attitudes. Martin Seligman's learned helplessness began with dogs that stopped trying to escape shock; it grew into the optimistic versus pessimistic explanatory style, which predicts health, longevity, performance and depression. Seligman then launched positive psychology, and the chapter closes by reviewing research on subjective well-being (money, attractiveness, health, age, marriage, culture, geography, ethnicity, personality, control, positive thinking, goals, success and Internet use), his three kinds of happiness, and his later concept of flourishing.
objectives: Explain what it means to study personality through limited-domain facets such as locus of control, sensation seeking and learned helplessness.

Distinguish internal from external locus of control, describe how it is assessed with the I-E Scale and the Nowicki-Strickland scale, and summarise research on age, gender, culture, behaviour, mental and physical health.
Describe the parental behaviours that foster an internal locus of control and compare locus of control with Bandura's self-efficacy.
Define sensation seeking, describe the Sensation Seeking Scale, its four components and Zuckerman's good versus bad sensation seeking.

Summarise differences between high and low sensation seekers in age, gender, race, behaviour, personality, cognition, occupational interests and attitudes, and evaluate the roles of heredity and environment.
Describe Seligman's discovery of learned helplessness and the early research with dogs and humans, including its misuse as torture.
Explain how learned helplessness affects emotional and physical health and how it relates to depression.

Distinguish optimistic and pessimistic explanatory styles (internal-stable-global versus external-unstable-specific attributions) and summarise their effects on health, longevity, performance and cognition, including the downside of optimism.
Explain how learned helplessness and explanatory style develop in childhood.
Describe Seligman's positive psychology, the meaning of subjective well-being, and the research on factors that are and are not related to happiness.
Distinguish the pleasant, engaged and meaningful lives, and explain Seligman's concept of flourishing and its five pillars.

sections.heading: The Limited-Domain Approach: Facets of Personality
sections.detailed:
This chapter belongs to the part of the book labelled the limited-domain approach, and its title calls its topics facets of personality. Rather than presenting a single theorist's all-embracing account of the whole personality, as Freud, Jung or Eysenck tried to do, the chapter takes three specific aspects of personality and follows the large research literature that has grown up around each one. The chapter itself describes Zuckerman's sensation seeking as a limited-domain aspect of personality and Seligman's learned helplessness as a limited-domain facet, which shows how the approach works: one carefully defined variable is measured objectively and then related to a wide range of behaviour.

The three facets are captured in the chapter's subtitle. Taking control refers to Julian Rotter's locus of control, the belief that reinforcements depend either on our own behaviour (internal) or on luck, fate and other people (external). Taking chances refers to Marvin Zuckerman's sensation seeking, the need for varied, novel, complex and intense experiences and the willingness to take risks to get them. Finding happiness refers to Martin Seligman's work, which moved from learned helplessness through the optimistic and pessimistic explanatory styles to positive psychology and the study of subjective well-being.

Common features of the three programmes are worth noting for exam answers. Each starts from a narrow, testable idea; each has its own measuring instrument (the I-E Scale, the Sensation Seeking Scale, measures of optimism and pessimism and of subjective well-being); each has been studied in many countries and age groups; and each links back to other chapters. Locus of control is compared with Bandura's self-efficacy, sensation seeking with Eysenck's extraversion and psychoticism and the five-factor model, and happiness with the five-factor traits and with internal control.

The chapter also shows a contrast in emphasis. Rotter's and Seligman's facets are presented as largely learned, especially through childhood experience and parenting, whereas Zuckerman stresses the strong hereditary basis of sensation seeking, which the chapter says puts his work in a different category from the behavioural and social-learning approaches. The result is a set of focused, research-heavy pictures of personality rather than one unified theory.
sections.simple: The limited-domain approach studies one specific piece of personality in depth instead of building a theory of the whole person. This chapter looks at three such pieces: Rotter's locus of control (taking control), Zuckerman's sensation seeking (taking chances), and Seligman's learned helplessness, optimism and happiness (finding happiness).
keyPoints: The chapter treats personality through narrow, well-defined facets rather than one grand theory.
Taking control = Rotter's locus of control; taking chances = Zuckerman's sensation seeking; finding happiness = Seligman's work.
The book calls sensation seeking a limited-domain aspect and learned helplessness a limited-domain facet of personality.
Each facet has its own assessment tool and a large cross-cultural research base.
Rotter and Seligman stress learning; Zuckerman stresses heredity.

sections.heading: Julian Rotter: Locus of Control
sections.detailed:
Julian Rotter (1916-2014) was born in Brooklyn, New York, the youngest of three brothers, and he later joked that the three of them matched Adler's descriptions of oldest, middle and 'fighting' youngest child. The family was comfortable until the 1929 economic depression, when his father lost his business. Rotter described this sudden change as pivotal: it gave him a lifelong concern with social injustice and taught him how strongly situational conditions shape personality and behaviour. That lesson foreshadows his later interest in how people perceive the control that outside forces have over their lives.

In high school Rotter read Freud and Adler and amused himself by interpreting his friends' dreams, which made him want to be a psychologist. Because there were few jobs in psychology, he first majored in chemistry at Brooklyn College, but after meeting Alfred Adler there he switched to psychology even though he knew it was impractical. He hoped for an academic career but was warned, both at Brooklyn College and in graduate school, that Jewish candidates could not get university posts regardless of their credentials, and he felt the warnings were justified.

After his Ph.D. from Indiana University he worked at a state mental hospital in Connecticut and served as an army psychologist during World War II. He then joined Ohio State University, where George Kelly directed the clinical psychology programme. At Ohio State Rotter developed his social-learning approach to personality and attracted many able graduate students; one of them remembered the period as the 'glory days', with Rotter and Kelly both refining their major theoretical works.

In 1963 Rotter moved to the University of Connecticut at Storrs. He received the American Psychological Association's Distinguished Scientific Contribution Award in 1988 and stayed physically and socially active, playing tennis, squash and weekly poker into his 80s. By his death in 2014 he was regarded as one of the most eminent psychologists of the twentieth century.

The biography matters for exams because two themes connect directly to his theory: the experience of losing financial security through forces beyond the family's control, and his social-learning view that behaviour is shaped by both external reinforcements and internal cognitions.
sections.simple: Rotter grew up in Brooklyn; when his father's business failed in the Depression he learned how much outside circumstances shape behaviour. He met Adler, became a psychologist, worked alongside George Kelly at Ohio State, and developed a social-learning approach that led to the idea of locus of control.
keyPoints: Born 1916 in Brooklyn; youngest of three brothers; died 2014.
Father's business failure in the 1929 Depression gave him a concern with social injustice and the power of situations.
Met Alfred Adler at Brooklyn College and switched from chemistry to psychology.
Faced prejudice against Jewish academics; worked in a mental hospital and the army before Ohio State with George Kelly.
Moved to University of Connecticut (1963); APA Distinguished Scientific Contribution Award (1988).

sections.heading: Internal versus External Control of Reinforcement
sections.detailed:
Rotter tried to explain behaviour by looking both outside the person, at external reinforcements, and inside, at cognitive processes. Through an extensive research programme he found that people differ in where they think their reinforcements come from. Some believe rewards depend on their own actions; others believe rewards are controlled by other people and outside forces. He named this belief locus of control.

People with an internal locus of control believe that the reinforcement they receive is controlled by their own behaviour and abilities. People with an external locus of control believe that other people, fate or luck determine their rewards, and they feel powerless in the face of outside forces. The key point for exams is that locus of control is a belief or expectancy about the source of reinforcement, not a measure of how much control a person actually has.

This belief has large consequences for behaviour. Externals, convinced that their own efforts and abilities make no difference to what they receive, see little point in trying to improve their circumstances; if they do not expect to control present or future events, effort seems pointless. Internals, by contrast, feel they have a firm grip on their lives and act accordingly.

The chapter lists a set of advantages reported for internals (Saric & Pahic, 2013). Internals perform better at work than externals; they resist attempts to influence them; they value their own skills more highly; and they are more alert to cues in the environment that they can use to guide their behaviour. They report lower anxiety, higher self-esteem and greater happiness, and they enjoy better mental and physical health than people high in external control.

These differences explain the review question about a tornado warning. An external would tend to feel nothing could be done, because outcomes seem to depend on fate or luck, whereas an internal would be more likely to take action to protect self, family and property, because internals believe their behaviour affects what happens to them and they attend to environmental cues. The rest of the Rotter material shows how this single dimension relates to age, gender, culture, work and study behaviour, mental and physical health, and child rearing.
sections.simple: Locus of control is a belief about who controls your rewards. Internals think their own actions and abilities decide what they get; externals think luck, fate or powerful others decide. Internals therefore try harder, do better at work and are generally healthier and happier.
keyPoints: Locus of control = a belief about the source of reinforcement (Rotter).
Internal: reinforcement depends on one's own behaviour and abilities.
External: reinforcement is controlled by other people, fate or luck; feel powerless.
Externals see little value in effort; internals act to shape their lives.
Internals: better job performance, resist influence, value their skills, alert to cues, lower anxiety, higher self-esteem, happier, healthier.

sections.heading: Assessment of Locus of Control
sections.detailed:
Rotter measured locus of control with self-report inventories. The best known is the Internal-External (I-E) Scale (Rotter, 1966), which contains 23 forced-choice items. Each item is a pair of statements, and the respondent chooses the one that better describes his or her own beliefs. In every pair one option expresses an internal belief and the other an external belief, and the chapter notes that it is easy to see which is which.

Table 14.1 gives sample pairs. For example, one pair contrasts the idea that many unhappy events are partly caused by bad luck with the idea that people's misfortunes come from their own mistakes; another contrasts the view that capable people who fail to become leaders have not used their opportunities with the view that leadership needs the right breaks. Other pairs deal with wars, respect, teachers' fairness and grades, and whether some people simply will not like you however hard you try. Choosing the luck, fate or chance option repeatedly produces a more external score.

A second widely used instrument is the Children's Nowicki-Strickland Internal-External Scale, a 40-item test that has been translated into about two dozen languages (Nowicki & Strickland, 1973; Strickland, 1989). There is also an adult form and a cartoon version for preschool children (Nowicki & Duke, 1983), so locus of control can be measured across the lifespan.

Researchers have also built variants of the I-E Scale to measure locus of control for particular behaviours, such as factors related to successful dieting and weight loss, and performance in a variety of situations. This shows that the concept can be applied both as a generalised expectancy and to specific domains. Later in the chapter, for instance, researchers measure internal academic locus of control and internal health locus of control.

For evaluation, the chapter later praises the I-E Scale as an objective measure that has generated a great deal of research and has been applied in clinical and educational settings.
sections.simple: Rotter's I-E Scale has 23 pairs of statements; you pick the one you agree with, and one choice in each pair is internal and the other external. Children are tested with the 40-item Nowicki-Strickland scale, which also has adult and cartoon preschool versions. Special versions measure control beliefs in areas such as dieting.
keyPoints: I-E Scale (Rotter, 1966): 23 forced-choice item pairs; one internal and one external option per pair.
Children's Nowicki-Strickland Internal-External Scale: 40 items, translated into about two dozen languages.
Adult form and a cartoon version for preschoolers exist (Nowicki & Duke, 1983).
Variants measure specific domains, e.g., dieting and weight loss, performance situations.
The scale is objective and has been used in clinical and educational settings.

sections.heading: Age and Gender Differences
sections.detailed:
Attempts to control the external environment begin in infancy and become more pronounced between the ages of 8 and 14. Locus of control then continues to change with age: people apparently grow more internally oriented as they get older, reaching a peak in middle age (Heckhausen & Schulz, 1995). College students in general have been found to show an internal rather than an external orientation.

Internal control can also be increased in later life. A study of men and women in the United States aged 60 to 75 found that cognitive training significantly improved their internal locus of control (Wolinsky et al., 2009). This finding is useful because it supports the idea that locus of control is a learned expectancy that can be modified, not a fixed trait.

Gender findings are mixed and vary by country, which is an important point to make in an answer. A study of 14- and 15-year-olds in Norway found that girls scored significantly higher than boys on internal locus of control (Manger & Ekeland, 2000). In the United States, no significant differences were found between adult men and women in overall I-E Scale scores (DeBrabander & Boone, 1990). However, a more recent study of 18- to 29-year-olds in England found that women were more external than men (Holland, Geraghty, & Shah, 2010), and in China men have scored higher than women in internal control (Tong & Wang, 2006).

Taken together, the research suggests a fairly consistent age trend (more internal with age up to middle age) but no universal gender difference. Where gender differences appear, their direction depends on the culture and age group studied, which points to social and cultural influences rather than a simple biological sex difference.
sections.simple: People become more internal as they grow up, peaking in middle age, and older adults can become more internal through cognitive training. Gender results are mixed: Norwegian teenage girls were more internal than boys, US adults showed no difference, but English young women and Chinese women were more external than men.
keyPoints: Control attempts start in infancy and increase between ages 8 and 14.
Internality increases with age, peaking in middle age (Heckhausen & Schulz, 1995); college students tend to be internal.
Cognitive training raised internal control in US adults aged 60-75 (Wolinsky et al., 2009).
Norway: girls more internal than boys (Manger & Ekeland, 2000); US adults: no gender difference (DeBrabander & Boone, 1990).
England (18-29): women more external (Holland et al., 2010); China: men more internal (Tong & Wang, 2006).

sections.heading: Cultural Differences
sections.detailed:
Ethnic group comparisons. Studies in Africa found that native Africans, like American-born Black people in general, scored higher in external control than American-born White people (Okeke, Draguns, Sheku, & Allen, 1999). In Botswana, Black adolescents of both sexes were more external than White adolescents in the United States, but in both countries teenagers of higher socioeconomic status were more internal than lower-status teens (Maqsud & Rouhani, 1991). This socioeconomic finding suggests that real access to resources shapes control beliefs.

A comparison of Caucasian, Hispanic, Asian and African-American teenagers found that having an internal locus of control was regarded as more important by the Caucasians than by the other groups (Kang, Chang, Chen, & Greenberger, 2015). In the Netherlands, immigrants from Morocco and Turkey scored much higher in external control than native-born Dutch people (van Dijk et al., 2013). Among Hispanic immigrants to the United States, those with a more internal locus of control adapted better to the demands of the new culture and coped better with discrimination and marginalisation (Llamas & Consoli, 2014).

Collectivist versus individualistic cultures. In general, Asians have been found to be more external than Americans. The chapter explains this through cultural values: American culture prizes self-reliance and individualism, whereas Asian cultures emphasise collectivism, reliance on the community and interdependence, so success is seen more as a product of external than internal factors. Contact with American culture shifts people toward internality: Chinese residents of Hong Kong were more external than Chinese Americans, who in turn were more external than European Americans (Uba, 1994).

A large comparison of 18 cultures confirmed that people in collectivist cultures such as China are more external than people in Westernised countries, who value internal control more (Cheng, Cheung, Chio, & Chan, 2013). Similarly, college students in South Africa, described as an individualistic culture, scored significantly more internal than students in Lebanon, a more collectivist and structured culture (Nasser & Abouchedid, 2006).

In summary, externality is more common among lower socioeconomic groups, some minority and immigrant groups, and collectivist cultures, while internality is associated with higher status, individualism and acculturation to Western society. The chapter's highlights box sums this up by saying that internals tend to live in wealthy individualistic cultures.
sections.simple: Black Africans, immigrant groups and people in collectivist Asian or Middle Eastern cultures tend to score more external, while wealthier and more individualistic groups score more internal. Higher socioeconomic status goes with internality everywhere, and the more contact Asians have with American culture, the more internal they become.
keyPoints: Native Africans and American-born Blacks more external than American-born Whites (Okeke et al., 1999).
Higher-SES teens more internal in both Botswana and the US (Maqsud & Rouhani, 1991).
Moroccan and Turkish immigrants in the Netherlands more external than natives; internal Hispanic immigrants adapt better to the US.
Collectivist cultures (Asia, China, Lebanon) more external than individualistic ones (US, South Africa).
Acculturation gradient: Hong Kong Chinese > Chinese Americans > European Americans in externality (Uba, 1994).

sections.heading: Behavioral Differences
sections.detailed:
Research across several countries shows that locus of control predicts how people behave at work, in study and in groups.

Work and sport. Studies of workers in China and of athletes in Sweden found that people high in internal control were better able to adapt to and commit to change, and they scored higher on tests of mental skills than more external people (Chen & Wang, 2007; Fallby, Hassmen, Kentta, & Durand-Burand, 2006). Other research found that internal locus of control at work was positively related to job satisfaction, job commitment and general life satisfaction (Wang, Bowling, & Eschleman, 2010).

Academic behaviour. The concept can be narrowed to academic locus of control, meaning the belief that one's own efforts will lead to doing well in school. In Korea, people high in internal academic locus of control were more likely to persist in an online college programme (Joo, Joung, & Sim, 2011). In Turkey, college students high in internal academic locus of control were far less likely to become addicted to Internet use than those low in it (Iskender & Akin, 2010).

Collective locus of control. Paralleling Bandura's idea of collective self-efficacy, the chapter suggests there may be a collective locus of control shared by groups who work or study together. Research on entrepreneurial work teams in Austria showed that teams with the highest internal locus of control performed far more efficiently and effectively than teams lower in internal control (Khan, Breitenecker, & Schwarz, 2014).

These findings illustrate the review question asking how internals behave differently from externals: internals adapt to change, show stronger mental skills, are more satisfied and committed at work, persist in study, resist Internet addiction and, as teams, perform better. The underlying reason is the same throughout: if you believe your actions produce outcomes, effort and persistence make sense.
sections.simple: Internals adapt better to change, have stronger mental skills, and are more satisfied and committed at work. Students with internal academic control persist in online courses and avoid Internet addiction, and whole teams with internal control perform better.
keyPoints: Chinese workers and Swedish athletes high in internality adapt to change and score higher on mental skills.
Internal control at work relates to job satisfaction, commitment and life satisfaction (Wang et al., 2010).
Korea: internal academic control predicts persistence in online college (Joo et al., 2011).
Turkey: internal academic control protects against Internet addiction (Iskender & Akin, 2010).
Collective locus of control: internal Austrian entrepreneurial teams performed better (Khan et al., 2014).

sections.heading: Mental Health Differences
sections.detailed:
People high in internal control are less likely to have emotional problems or to become alcoholics, and they cope better with stress. A study of nurses in Germany showed that those reporting more work-related stress and burnout scored higher in external control than nurses less troubled by stress and burnout (Owen, 2006; Schmitz, Neumann, & Oppermann, 2000).

Research on diverse groups, including pregnant women, female prisoners and police officers, found that people high in external control are more prone to fantasies, anxiety, depression, fear of death on the job (among police), psychotic episodes and hopelessness. Externals were also more likely to become victims of cyberbullying (Ariso & Reyero, 2014; Asberg & Renk, 2014; and others).

Adjustment to new situations also depends on locus of control. College students in Greece, a family-oriented and highly protective culture, were followed as they left home, many for the first time; those high in internal control adjusted more readily (Leontopoulou, 2006). First-year college students in Turkey who were high in external control were far more indecisive in new situations (Bacanli, 2006).

High external control has been linked with compulsive hoarding (Benson-Townsend & Silver, 2014), and people with various addictions benefit from therapy when they develop a more internal locus of control (Amram & Benbenishty, 2014), which implies that control beliefs can be changed therapeutically. Internals experience less anxiety and depression, are less likely to be lonely or to attempt suicide, and find greater meaning in life.

A striking natural-stress study involved Israeli teenagers during the 1990 Persian Gulf War, when Scud missile attacks caused widespread injury and destruction. Adolescents higher in perceived control experienced significantly less anxiety and fewer stress-related symptoms than those lower in perceived control (Zeidner, 1993). Finally, internals show higher levels of mental health, more meaningful lives and higher subjective well-being than externals (Shojaee & French, 2014; Singh & Choudhri, 2014), which links Rotter's work to the later happiness research in the chapter.
sections.simple: Internals have fewer emotional problems, cope better with stress, adjust better to new situations and are less anxious, depressed, lonely or suicidal. Externals are more prone to burnout, anxiety, hopelessness, cyberbullying victimisation, indecision and hoarding, and addicts improve when therapy makes them more internal.
keyPoints: Internals: fewer emotional problems, less alcoholism, better coping with stress (German nurses study).
Externals: more fantasies, anxiety, depression, psychotic episodes, hopelessness, cyberbullying victimisation.
Greek students adjusting to leaving home and Turkish first-years: internals adjust better and are less indecisive.
External control linked to hoarding; developing internality helps addiction therapy.
Israeli teens in the 1990 Gulf War: high perceived control = less anxiety and stress (Zeidner, 1993).

sections.heading: Physical Health Differences
sections.detailed:
Internally oriented people tend to be physically healthier than externals, with lower blood pressure and fewer heart attacks. When internals do develop cardiac problems, they cooperate better with hospital staff and are discharged sooner; a Norwegian study found they also return to work sooner than externals (Bergvik, Sorlie, & Wynn, 2012).

Among patients recovering from coronary artery bypass surgery, those high in internal control had reached higher physical functioning at six weeks and six months after surgery (Barry et al., 2006). Among older cancer patients in the Netherlands, internals experienced less depression than externals (Aarts et al., 2015).

Health behaviour helps explain these results. Several studies show that internals are more careful about their health: they are more likely to wear seat belts, eat well, exercise regularly and quit smoking (Cobb-Clark et al., 2014; Phares, 1993; Seeman, Seeman, & Sayles, 1985; Segall & Wynd, 1990). In Nigeria, internals were more likely to have screening for cervical and breast cancer (Adebimpe & Oladimeji, 2014). In the Netherlands, cancer patients high in external control placed more trust in their oncologists (Hillen et al., 2014), which fits the external belief that powerful others control outcomes.

The findings are not entirely one-sided. Studies in France, Germany and South Africa found that people high in internal health locus of control took less care of their health in general, although they had fewer eating disorders and engaged in fewer behaviours that put them at risk for HIV (Grotz et al., 2011; Gwandure & Mayekiso, 2010; Scoffier et al., 2010). This mixed result is worth mentioning in a balanced answer.

Finally, research in Sweden found that up to one-third of older people, people with little formal education and immigrant groups scored low in internal health locus of control (Lindstrom, 2011), echoing the earlier link between disadvantage and externality. Overall, the chapter's highlights conclude that internals tend to be physically healthy.
sections.simple: Internals have lower blood pressure, fewer heart attacks, cooperate better in hospital, recover faster after heart surgery and go back to work sooner. They usually look after their health (seat belts, diet, exercise, quitting smoking, cancer screening), though a few studies found internals took less general care of their health while still having fewer eating disorders and HIV-risk behaviours.
keyPoints: Internals: lower blood pressure, fewer heart attacks, better cooperation in hospital, earlier discharge and return to work.
Bypass patients high in internality functioned better at 6 weeks and 6 months (Barry et al., 2006).
Internals wear seat belts, eat well, exercise, quit smoking and get cancer screening (Nigeria).
Externals trust their oncologists more (Hillen et al., 2014).
Mixed: high internal health locus of control linked to less general health care but fewer eating disorders and HIV-risk behaviours.

sections.heading: Developing Locus of Control in Childhood
sections.detailed:
Evidence suggests that locus of control is learned in childhood and is directly related to parental behaviour (Ahlin & Lobo Antunes, 2015). This makes it a social-learning variable, consistent with Rotter's overall approach.

Family conditions that foster externality. Children raised in homes without an adult male role model are likely to express external control beliefs, and external beliefs tend to increase with the number of siblings. Children in large single-parent families headed by women were more likely to develop an external locus of control (Schneewind, 1995). Later research found that children whose mothers are depressed and have little formal education or income are likely to become external (Freed & Tompson, 2011). Children from low-income families have a lower sense of control in all areas of their lives than children from higher-income families (Mittal & Griskevicius, 2014). The common thread is a home environment where resources, attention and predictable responses are limited.

Parenting that fosters internality. Parents of children with an internal locus of control were found to be highly supportive; they praised achievements, which is positive reinforcement; they were consistent in their discipline; and they were not authoritarian. As the children grew older, these parents continued to build an internal orientation by encouraging independence. Each of these features makes sense in social-learning terms: consistent, contingent consequences teach a child that his or her behaviour reliably produces outcomes, and independence gives the child chances to experience that control directly.

This material answers the review question on parental behaviours that foster internal control: support, praise for achievement, consistent discipline, a non-authoritarian style and encouragement of independence. The chapter's highlights box adds that internals tend to have parents who are themselves high in internal control.
sections.simple: Locus of control is learned from parents. Children become more external when there is no father figure, many siblings, a depressed or poorly educated mother, or low family income. Parents who are supportive, praise success, discipline consistently, avoid being authoritarian and encourage independence raise internal children.
keyPoints: Locus of control is learned in childhood and tied to parental behaviour.
External risk factors: no adult male role model, more siblings, large female-headed single-parent families.
Depressed, poorly educated, low-income mothers and low family income predict externality.
Parents of internals: supportive, praise achievement, consistent discipline, not authoritarian.
These parents encourage independence as the child grows.

sections.heading: Reflections on Locus of Control
sections.detailed:
Relation to self-efficacy. A large research programme with college students and sales representatives found a strong relationship between Rotter's locus of control and Bandura's self-efficacy (Judge, Erez, Bono, & Thoresen, 2002). Some researchers argue that both concepts concern our perception or belief about how much control we have over the events in our lives and our ability to cope with them; this is their similarity. A major difference is that locus of control is a generalised belief that applies across many situations, whereas self-efficacy tends to be specific to a particular situation.

Bandura himself insisted that the overlap is small. His argument is that believing you can carry out a certain action (self-efficacy) is not the same as believing that actions affect outcomes (locus of control). Put simply, self-efficacy is about 'can I do it?', while locus of control is about 'will doing it make a difference to what I get?'. A person could believe that effort pays off in general but doubt that he or she can perform a particular task, or vice versa.

Evaluation. The chapter's assessment of Rotter is very positive. His research was rigorous and well controlled, and he used objective measures wherever possible. Studies have given considerable empirical support to the concept. The I-E Scale has generated a large body of research and has been applied in clinical and educational settings. Rotter himself observed that locus of control had become one of the most studied variables in psychology, and research on it continues well into the twenty-first century.

Highlights of research. The chapter summarises that people high in internal control tend to live in wealthy individualistic cultures, perform well at school, avoid Internet addiction, have high job and life satisfaction, have low anxiety and depression, cope better with stress, be physically healthy, and have parents who are high in internal control.
sections.simple: Locus of control is strongly related to Bandura's self-efficacy, since both deal with perceived control, but locus of control is general while self-efficacy is situation-specific, and Bandura argued they are different ideas. Rotter's work is praised as rigorous, objective and hugely influential.
keyPoints: Strong empirical link between locus of control and self-efficacy (Judge et al., 2002).
Similarity: both concern perceived control over life events and ability to cope.
Difference: locus of control is generalised across situations; self-efficacy is situation-specific.
Bandura: belief that one can perform an action differs from belief that actions affect outcomes.
Rotter's research is rigorous, objective, well supported; locus of control is one of the most studied variables.

sections.heading: Marvin Zuckerman: Sensation Seeking
sections.detailed:
Beginning in the 1970s, Marvin Zuckerman (born 1928) of the University of Delaware has researched a limited-domain aspect of personality that he calls sensation seeking. The chapter notes that the trait has a large hereditary component, something first observed by Eysenck, and this biological emphasis becomes a recurring theme in Zuckerman's work.

Zuckerman defines sensation seeking as a desire for varied, novel, complex and intense sensations and experiences, together with a willingness to take physical, social, legal and financial risks for the sake of those experiences (Zuckerman, 1994a). The glossary definition is shorter: the need for varied, novel and complex sensations and experiences. The chapter suggests the everyday label 'taking chances'.

Two parts of the definition deserve emphasis in an exam answer. The first is the type of stimulation sought: experiences that are varied rather than repetitive, novel rather than familiar, complex rather than simple, and intense rather than mild. The second is the willingness to accept risk, and the definition names four kinds: physical (for example, dangerous sports), social (for example, unconventional behaviour), legal (for example, illicit drug use) and financial (for example, gambling). Much of the later research follows exactly these lines, linking high sensation seeking to dangerous sports, drug and alcohol use, crime, risky sex, fast driving and gambling.

It is important to see sensation seeking as a dimension on which everyone can be placed, with high and low sensation seekers at the two ends. Low sensation seekers are not simply lacking something; the chapter later shows that they have their own characteristic profile, such as preferring the familiar, being more authoritarian and having less tolerance for ambiguity, and describing themselves with words such as fearful and worried.

Sensation seeking therefore provides the 'taking chances' facet of the chapter, complementing Rotter's 'taking control' and Seligman's 'finding happiness'.
sections.simple: Zuckerman, at the University of Delaware since the 1970s, studies sensation seeking: the need for varied, new, complex and intense experiences and a readiness to take physical, social, legal and financial risks to get them. It is largely inherited and can be summed up as 'taking chances'.
keyPoints: Marvin Zuckerman (1928-), University of Delaware, research from the 1970s.
Sensation seeking: need for varied, novel, complex and intense sensations and experiences.
Includes willingness to take physical, social, legal and financial risks.
Trait has a large hereditary component, first noted by Eysenck.
Popular label: 'taking chances'; people range from low to high.

sections.heading: Assessing Sensation Seeking
sections.detailed:
To measure the trait, Zuckerman built the Sensation Seeking Scale (SSS), a 40-item paper-and-pencil questionnaire. He validated it by giving it to people whose behaviour fitted his definition: volunteers for psychological experiments involving novel experiences, people in physically dangerous jobs such as police officers and race-car drivers, and people who admitted experimenting with drugs or varied sexual experiences. Their scores were compared with those of people who deliberately avoided novel or risky activities. As predicted, the deliberate seekers of unusual activities scored high and the less venturesome scored low, which supports the test's validity.

The SSS uses a forced-choice format like Rotter's I-E Scale. Table 14.2 shows sample items from Form V, where the respondent picks the preferred statement in each pair: wild uninhibited parties versus quiet parties with good conversation; getting bored with the same old faces versus liking the comfort of familiar friends; trying parachute jumping versus never wanting to jump from a plane; travelling without a planned route versus carefully planning one; enjoying sexy scenes in films versus objecting to them; and dressing individually even if it looks strange versus dressing to a standard of taste. The test has been revised several times and is now in its fifth version, and there is a version for children.

Other scales. Sensation seeking measures have been developed in the United States and elsewhere. German psychologists published the Need Inventory of Sensation Seeking in German and English (Roth & Hammelstein, 2012), and later research suggested it might be even more reliable and valid than Zuckerman's original scale (Marker & Schneider, 2015). In China the Brief Sensation Seeking Scale has proved reliable and valid in predicting reckless motorcycle riding, excessive alcohol and cigarette use, and risky sexual behaviour (Chen et al., 2013; Fan et al., 2014).

The availability of several reliable instruments in different languages helps explain why sensation seeking has been studied so widely across cultures and age groups, as the following sections show.
sections.simple: Zuckerman's Sensation Seeking Scale (SSS) is a 40-item forced-choice questionnaire, validated by showing that risk-takers score high and cautious people score low; it is now in its fifth version with a children's form. Other measures include the German Need Inventory of Sensation Seeking and China's Brief Sensation Seeking Scale.
keyPoints: SSS: 40-item paper-and-pencil, forced-choice questionnaire; now Form V; children's version exists.
Validated with experiment volunteers, police and race-car drivers, drug and sex experimenters vs risk-avoiders.
Sample items: wild parties vs quiet parties, parachuting, unplanned travel, individual dress.
Need Inventory of Sensation Seeking (Roth & Hammelstein, 2012) may be more reliable and valid than the SSS.
Brief Sensation Seeking Scale (China) predicts reckless motorcycling, alcohol/cigarette use, risky sex.

sections.heading: Components of Sensation Seeking; Good and Bad Sensation Seeking
sections.detailed:
Using factor analysis, Zuckerman (1983; Zuckerman & Aluja, 2015) identified four components of sensation seeking. These four are among the most frequently asked points in this chapter.

1. Thrill and adventure seeking: a desire for physical activities involving speed, danger, novelty and defiance of gravity, such as parachuting, scuba diving or bungee jumping.

2. Experience seeking: the search for novel experiences through travel, music, art or a nonconformist lifestyle shared with similarly inclined people. This is the mental and sensory side of the trait rather than the physical side.

3. Disinhibition: the need to seek release in uninhibited social activities, including risky sex, impulsiveness, aggressiveness and antisocial behaviour.

4. Boredom susceptibility: a dislike of repetitive experiences, routine work and predictable people, with restless discontent when exposed to such situations.

Good and bad sensation seeking. Zuckerman later distinguished two types (Roberti, 2004; Zuckerman, 1994b). The good type, called non-impulsive socialized sensation seeking, involves the thrill and adventure seeking component; such a person might channel the need for stimulation into demanding but socially acceptable activities. The bad type, called impulsive unsocialized sensation seeking, consists of high scores on disinhibition, experience seeking and boredom susceptibility, together with high scores on Eysenck's psychoticism scale. The link with psychoticism signals the asocial, impulsive quality of this form.

The distinction matters because sensation seeking itself is not presented as good or bad; what matters is whether the need for stimulation is expressed in a controlled, socially acceptable form or in an impulsive and antisocial one. The later research on drug use, crime and risky sex mostly reflects the unsocialized form, while involvement in adventurous sports reflects the socialized form. The chapter also reports that gender differences appear on the separate components: men score higher on thrill and adventure seeking, disinhibition and boredom susceptibility, while women score higher on experience seeking.
sections.simple: Factor analysis gave four components: thrill and adventure seeking (dangerous physical activities), experience seeking (new experiences through travel, art, music, lifestyle), disinhibition (wild, uninhibited social behaviour) and boredom susceptibility (hating routine). Good sensation seeking is socialized and non-impulsive (thrill and adventure seeking); bad sensation seeking is impulsive and unsocialized (high disinhibition, experience seeking, boredom susceptibility and psychoticism).
keyPoints: Four components identified by factor analysis.
Thrill and adventure seeking: speed, danger, defiance of gravity (parachuting, scuba, bungee).
Experience seeking: novelty via travel, music, art, nonconformist lifestyle.
Disinhibition: risky sex, impulsiveness, aggression, antisocial acts; boredom susceptibility: aversion to routine and predictable people.
Good = non-impulsive socialized (thrill/adventure); bad = impulsive unsocialized (disinhibition, experience seeking, boredom susceptibility, high psychoticism).

sections.heading: Characteristics of Sensation Seekers
sections.detailed:
Age differences. Differences in sensation seeking appear very early. In a study of US second-graders, high scorers chose to watch a video about scary sharks, while low scorers chose one about a funny bunny (Trice, 2010). In general, younger people seek adventure, risk and novelty more than older people. Among high school and college students in the United States and Canada, high sensation seekers were more likely to engage in reckless and risky behaviour and uncontrolled gambling (Collado et al., 2014; George et al., 2006; Gupta et al., 2006). Testing from adolescence to age 60 showed that sensation seeking rises during the middle school years and falls in the twenties (Lynne-Landsman, Graber, Nichols, & Botvin, 2011). Educational level made no difference: college students did not score significantly higher or lower than people who had not attended college.

Zuckerman's own experience. Zuckerman said his own life confirmed the age research. As a college student he felt he reached his full sensation-seeking potential through drinking, sex and hitch-hiking around the country. At 74 he wrote that he had once imagined taking up hang gliding, parachuting and flying after retirement, but that thrill and adventure seeking and disinhibition fall rapidly with age while experience seeking does not change. He reported still seeking new experiences, though less physically adventurous ones. This gives a useful detail for exams: not all components decline equally with age.

Gender differences. In countries as different as the United States and Iran, men consistently score higher in sensation seeking and lower in impulse control than women (Khodarahimi, 2014; Shulman et al., 2015). On the components, men score higher on thrill and adventure seeking, disinhibition and boredom susceptibility, while women score higher on experience seeking. Similar results came from the United States, England, Scotland, Japan and Thailand.

Racial and cultural differences. Asians score lower on the SSS than people in Western countries, and White subjects score higher than non-Whites. The chapter summary therefore lists Whites, males, people from Western cultures and young people from adolescence to the early twenties as the groups highest in sensation seeking.
sections.simple: Sensation seeking shows up even in young children, rises in middle school and drops in the twenties; thrill seeking and disinhibition decline with age, but experience seeking does not. Men score higher overall (and on thrill seeking, disinhibition and boredom susceptibility), women higher on experience seeking, and Westerners and Whites score higher than Asians and non-Whites.
keyPoints: Second-graders high in sensation seeking chose the shark video over the funny bunny (Trice, 2010).
Rises in middle school, declines in the twenties; education level makes no difference.
Zuckerman: thrill/adventure seeking and disinhibition fall with age; experience seeking does not.
Men higher overall and on thrill seeking, disinhibition, boredom susceptibility; women higher on experience seeking.
Asians lower than Westerners; Whites higher than non-Whites.

sections.heading: Behavioral Differences: Risk Taking, Drugs, Driving and Sex
sections.detailed:
Physical risk taking. Skydivers, firefighters, riot-control police, bungee jumpers and race-car drivers score higher on the SSS than groups who do not do these things. Among American Motocross drivers, the most experienced (those in the most races) had the highest sensation-seeking scores (Smith, Bissett, & Russo, 2014). Male undergraduates in Israel who were high sensation seekers were more likely to take part in risky sports and to volunteer for military combat units (Hobfoll, Rom, & Segal, 1989).

Different types of risk taking. Levenson (1990) identified three types of risk takers: antisocial (for example, drug addicts and criminals), adventurous (for example, mountain climbers and skydivers) and pro-social (for example, police officers and firefighters). Antisocial and adventurous risk takers had significantly higher SSS scores than pro-social risk takers, whose motives seem to involve something other than thrill and adventure seeking. High sensation seekers are also more willing to move from familiar to unfamiliar surroundings and to travel to exotic places even when the journey is hazardous.

Drugs, drinking, crime, fast cars and online poker. High sensation seekers are more likely to use and sell illicit drugs, and to start at an earlier age, to drink alcohol, to shoplift and to commit delinquent acts. These results came from Black children in the United States aged 9 to 15, South African university students, American high school students and adults, and Norwegian teenagers. American high school and college students high in sensation seeking were more likely to smoke, drink, use drugs, drive fast, have more car accidents and convictions for reckless or drunk driving, and have frequent sex. Studies in Spain and France confirmed the link with speeding and drunk driving. In France, online poker players scored higher in sensation seeking and felt strong arousal while playing (Barrault & Varesconi, 2013).

Risky sexual behaviour. Young Black women in the United States (15 to 21) high in sexual sensation seeking reported more sexual risk taking, such as more partners and less condom use (Spitalnick et al., 2007). In Zuckerman's research, 16 percent of high sensation seekers reported risky homosexual encounters compared with 7 percent of low sensation seekers, and among college men high scores correlated with risky sex they knew could expose them to AIDS; older subjects showed the same pattern. The link among gay men, both Black and White, was so strong that researchers concluded high-sensation-seeking males are a high-risk group for AIDS (Fisher & Misovich, 1990; Kalichman et al., 1994).
sections.simple: High sensation seekers are found in dangerous jobs and sports, volunteer for combat, and travel to risky places. They are more likely to use drugs and alcohol, shoplift, drive fast and drunk, gamble online and take sexual risks; antisocial and adventurous risk takers score higher than pro-social ones like firefighters.
keyPoints: Skydivers, firefighters, riot police, bungee jumpers and race-car drivers score high; experienced Motocross riders score highest.
Levenson (1990): antisocial and adventurous risk takers score higher than pro-social risk takers.
Linked to earlier and greater drug use and dealing, drinking, shoplifting, delinquency across many countries.
Fast and drunk driving, accidents and convictions (US, Spain, France); online poker in France.
Risky sex: 16% vs 7% risky encounters; high-sensation-seeking gay men a high-risk group for AIDS.

sections.heading: Behavioral Differences: Cheating, Colors, Tattoos, Computer Use and Job Performance
sections.detailed:
Beyond dramatic risk taking, high and low sensation seekers differ in many everyday behaviours.

Cheating, color choices and tattoos. Studies in Israel found that high sensation seekers are more likely to cross a street on foot against a red light, and they prefer 'hot' colours such as red and orange over pastels such as light blue (Rosenbloom, 2006a, 2006b). In Germany, among 14- to 24-year-olds, significantly more high sensation seekers had tattoos and body piercings (Stirn, Hinz, & Braehler, 2006). American college students high in sensation seeking were more likely to cheat on academic tests (DeAndrea et al., 2009).

Computer use. High school and college students in China who were high sensation seekers were more likely to become obsessed with computer games and Internet use. American workers high in sensation seeking often used workplace computers for personal purposes such as emailing, playing games and viewing sexual websites (Everton, Mastrangelo, & Jolton, 2005). However, research with American college students did not support a relationship between sensation seeking and computer misuse (Velezmoro, Lacefield, & Roberti, 2010), so this finding is not fully consistent.

Job performance. In a study of 233 low-level US employees, high sensation seekers had lower job performance than low sensation seekers. They were also less likely to build social relationships at work or to seek information from co-workers and supervisors. The researchers suggested that such low-level jobs may not provide enough stimulation for high sensation seekers (Reio & Sanders-Reio, 2006). This links to the later section on occupational preferences, which shows that high sensation seekers are drawn to varied, stimulating work.

Together with the previous section, these findings answer the review question asking for examples of how high sensation seekers behave differently: they take physical, legal and sexual risks, prefer intense colours, have more tattoos and piercings, cheat more, may misuse computers, and perform poorly in dull jobs.
sections.simple: High sensation seekers jaywalk against red lights, like hot colours, have more tattoos and piercings, and cheat more on tests. They may get hooked on computer games or misuse work computers (though not all studies agree), and they do worse in boring low-level jobs.
keyPoints: Israel: cross against red lights; prefer hot colours (red, orange) over pastels.
Germany (14-24): more tattoos and body piercings.
US college students: more academic cheating.
China: obsession with games and Internet; US workers misuse work computers; not supported for US college students.
233 low-level US employees: high sensation seekers performed worse and formed fewer work relationships (jobs too unstimulating).

sections.heading: Personality Differences
sections.detailed:
Zuckerman and others correlated SSS scores with many personality factors.

Eysenck's factors and egocentric extraversion. SSS scores, especially on disinhibition, were related to Eysenck's extraversion and to the asocial tendencies of psychoticism. From this Zuckerman suggested that high sensation seekers are egocentrically extraverted: they are interested in other people mainly as an audience or as a source of stimulation, and they do not relate to others in a dependent or nurturing way. This is an important qualification, because it shows that their sociability is not the warm, affiliative kind.

Jung's extraversion. High SSS scores also correlated positively with extraversion as described by Carl Jung and measured by the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (Morehouse, Farley, & Youngquist, 1990).

Neuroticism. Studies found no correlation between sensation seeking and neuroticism. Zuckerman concluded that high SSS scores do not point to abnormal or neurotic behaviour, and he suggested that neuroses such as phobias and obsessive-compulsive behaviour might instead be related to low sensation seeking.

Five-factor and HEXACO models. Research on college students and adults in the Netherlands found that high sensation seekers scored high on openness to experience, extraversion and conscientiousness (three of the Big Five) and on two HEXACO factors, emotionality and honesty-humility (de Vries, de Vries, & Feij, 2009). Roberti (2004) also reported positive correlations with openness to experience and agreeableness.

Autonomy and nonconformity. High scorers show a high degree of autonomy. They express their emotions openly, are assertive, nonconforming and confirmed risk takers. They act independently of social conventions and of other people's needs and attitudes; governed mainly by their own needs, they arrange their lives to maximise chances for self-fulfilment.

Self-descriptions. Table 14.3 lists the adjectives high and low sensation seekers chose for themselves: high sensation seekers picked words such as enthusiastic, playful, adventurous, elated, imaginative, daring, zany and mischievous, while low sensation seekers chose frightened, panicky, tense, nervous, shaky, fearful, worried and upset.
sections.simple: High sensation seekers are extraverted (in Eysenck's and Jung's sense) but egocentrically so, using others as an audience; they tend toward psychoticism but not neuroticism. They score high on openness, extraversion and conscientiousness, are autonomous, assertive, nonconforming and emotionally expressive, and describe themselves as adventurous and playful while low scorers call themselves fearful and tense.
keyPoints: SSS (especially disinhibition) relates to Eysenck's extraversion and psychoticism.
Egocentric extraversion: others valued only as audience or stimulation, not in a nurturing way.
Positive correlation with Jungian extraversion (MBTI); no correlation with neuroticism; neuroses may go with low sensation seeking.
High openness, extraversion, conscientiousness (Big Five); high emotionality and honesty-humility (HEXACO); Roberti adds agreeableness.
Autonomous, assertive, nonconforming, emotionally expressive; self-descriptions: daring, playful vs fearful, tense.

sections.heading: Cognitive Processes
sections.detailed:
Intelligence. Correlations between sensation seeking and intelligence test scores are generally positive but not high. A study in the Republic of Mauritius found that children who scored high in sensation seeking at age 3 scored 12 points higher on intelligence tests at age 11 than children who were low in sensation seeking at age 3. This held for boys and girls and was not explained by parents' occupation or education (Raine, Reynolds, Venables, & Mednick, 2002). One interpretation consistent with the concept is that seeking stimulation exposes a child to more learning experiences.

School grades. Despite this, high sensation seekers did not earn better grades. Zuckerman suggested that because they spend more time on active recreation, they have less time for study.

Creativity and unusual ideas. Tests of creativity and originality showed that high sensation seekers have a greater capacity for original thinking, although they do not always show it in their schoolwork. High SSS scorers seem attracted to speculative, bizarre and even pseudoscientific ideas.

Primary-process thought. High sensation seekers also tend to engage in what Freud called primary-process thought. Their images, dreams and daydreams can be so vivid that the line between these inner stimuli and the real world becomes blurred. Zuckerman's explanation follows directly from the trait: because high sensation seekers constantly search for novelty, when they cannot find it in the outside world they may turn inward and create a fantasy world.

Perception. The chapter summary (p. 404) adds two further cognitive findings: high sensation seekers recognise symbols and figures more quickly and prefer complexity in visual stimulation. The summary also notes that they show stronger physiological responses to novel stimuli.

These points answer the cognitive half of the review question on how high and low sensation seekers differ in personality and cognitive functioning: modestly higher intelligence, no better grades, more originality, attraction to unusual ideas, vivid fantasy life, quicker symbol recognition and a preference for visual complexity.
sections.simple: Sensation seeking is mildly linked to higher intelligence; Mauritian children high in sensation seeking at 3 had IQs 12 points higher at 11. But high scorers don't get better grades, because they spend time on activities instead of study. They are more original, like bizarre ideas, have vivid fantasy lives, recognise figures quickly and prefer visual complexity.
keyPoints: Positive but low correlation with intelligence.
Mauritius: high sensation seekers at age 3 scored 12 IQ points higher at age 11 (Raine et al., 2002).
No better school grades: less time for study due to active recreation.
More original thinking; attracted to speculative, bizarre, pseudoscientific ideas; Freudian primary-process thought.
Summary: quicker recognition of symbols and figures, preference for visual complexity, stronger physiological response to novelty.

sections.heading: Occupational Preferences
sections.detailed:
Because high sensation seekers need varied and stimulating experiences, they tend to choose different jobs from low sensation seekers, and vocational interest tests show significant differences between the two groups.

On the Kuder Occupational Interest Survey, high SSS scores correlated positively with scientific interests and negatively with clerical interests. Men with high SSS scores also scored high on the Strong Interest Inventory scales for the helping professions, such as psychologist, physician, psychiatrist, social worker and minister. Their scores correlated negatively with business occupations such as accountant, purchasing agent and banker.

Women with high SSS scores showed high interest in the profession of lawyer and low interest in being an elementary school teacher.

An important qualification is that high sensation seekers of both sexes who were interested in the helping professions preferred the risky, cutting-edge parts of those fields, such as crisis intervention work or paramedic duty on emergency response teams. In other words, their interest in helping others is expressed through jobs that also provide intensity and unpredictability.

The chapter summary condenses this: the vocational interests of high-sensation-seeking males are oriented toward science and the helping professions, whereas low-sensation-seeking males lean toward clerical and business work. This links back to the job performance study, where high sensation seekers did poorly in low-level, unstimulating jobs, and to the highlights box, which says high sensation seekers tend to be interested in helping professions rather than business.
sections.simple: High sensation seekers prefer scientific work and dislike clerical work. High-scoring men like helping professions (psychologist, physician, social worker) but not business jobs (accountant, banker); high-scoring women like law but not elementary teaching. Within helping jobs, they prefer risky roles like crisis work or paramedic duty.
keyPoints: Kuder survey: high SSS correlates positively with scientific and negatively with clerical interests.
Men (Strong Interest Inventory): interest in psychologist, physician, psychiatrist, social worker, minister.
Men: negative correlation with accountant, purchasing agent, banker.
Women: high interest in lawyer, low in elementary school teacher.
Both sexes prefer risky helping roles: crisis intervention, paramedic emergency teams.

sections.heading: Attitudes
sections.detailed:
High sensation seekers tend to hold more liberal political and religious attitudes than low sensation seekers. They are more likely to express atheistic views than belief in a conventional religion, and they hold more permissive attitudes toward sexual behaviour, both their own and other people's (Zuckerman, 1994a).

Low sensation seekers show the opposite pattern. They are more likely to attend church frequently, and they score high on authoritarianism, a personality style typically marked by rigid opinions and prejudiced attitudes. They also show low tolerance for ambiguity: they regard ambiguous ideas and situations as threats rather than challenges.

The chapter summary (p. 404) restates this from the high end: high sensation seekers are higher in tolerance for ambiguity, more permissive in sexual attitudes and lower in authoritarianism.

These attitude differences fit the core of the trait. Someone who seeks novel, complex and varied experiences is likely to welcome unconventional ideas, to be open to uncertain situations and to reject rigid rules; someone who avoids novelty is likely to prefer clear, traditional and predictable belief systems. This material answers the review question asking about the political attitudes of high sensation seekers.
sections.simple: High sensation seekers are more liberal in politics and religion, more often atheist, and more permissive about sex. Low sensation seekers go to church more, score high on authoritarianism (rigid, prejudiced opinions) and see ambiguity as a threat rather than a challenge.
keyPoints: High sensation seekers: liberal political and religious attitudes, more atheistic.
More permissive sexual attitudes for self and others.
Low sensation seekers: frequent churchgoers, high authoritarianism.
Authoritarianism: rigid opinions and prejudiced attitudes.
Low sensation seekers have low tolerance for ambiguity, seeing it as a threat.

sections.heading: Heredity versus Environment
sections.detailed:
Heredity. A large body of research shows a strong hereditary basis for sensation seeking (Zuckerman, 2013). Eysenck (1983) estimated that 58 percent of the trait could be accounted for by genetic factors, and a twin study by Zuckerman and Sybil Eysenck found an even larger genetic component (Zuckerman, 1993). The chapter summary therefore calls sensation seeking primarily inherited.

Culture and learning. Environmental influence still matters. A comparison of 14- to 20-year-olds in Turkey and Wales found small but significant cultural differences in motivation to take risks, pointing to the role of learning (Kloep et al., 2009).

Parents. Zuckerman also recognised situational influences such as parental sensation seeking. Low-sensation-seeking parents may be overly fearful, protective and inhibiting, forbidding adventurous activities. High-sensation-seeking parents may encourage and reinforce unusual activities, creating an environment that promotes further sensation seeking.

Other childhood environments. A Swedish study found that teenagers equally high in impulsivity and sensation seeking committed fewer crimes if they attended more privileged schools (Eklund & Fritzell, 2014). Children raised in orphanages or other institutional care who were high in sensation seeking were much less likely to get into trouble than equally high scorers raised in private homes (Loman et al., 2014). These studies suggest the environment influences how the trait is expressed.

Birth order. Early SSS studies suggested that first-borns and only children of both sexes are higher in sensation seeking than later-borns. Zuckerman (1979) explained this by the greater stimulation and attention these children receive from parents early in life, which gives them a higher optimal level of stimulation. However, later research in England found no correlation between birth order and sensation seeking (Crozier & Birdsea, 2003).

Conclusion. Sensation seeking is mainly genetic, but cultural learning, parental modelling and reinforcement, school and home settings, and possibly birth order can shape its level and its expression. This is the balanced answer to the review question on heredity versus environment.
sections.simple: Sensation seeking is mostly inherited: Eysenck estimated 58 percent genetic, and a twin study found even more. Environment still matters: cultural differences, parents who encourage or forbid adventure, privileged schools and institutional care all affect how it shows, and early studies (not later ones) linked it to being first-born or an only child.
keyPoints: Strong hereditary basis; Eysenck (1983): 58 percent genetic; Zuckerman and Sybil Eysenck twin study: even higher.
Turkey vs Wales: small but significant cultural differences suggest learning matters.
Low-SS parents inhibit; high-SS parents reinforce adventurous behaviour.
Privileged schools (Sweden) and institutional care reduced trouble among high sensation seekers.
First-borns/only-borns higher in early studies (more early stimulation), but not replicated in England.

sections.heading: Reflections on Sensation Seeking
sections.detailed:
Zuckerman's focus on sensation seeking continues to generate research, and the trait has been linked to a wide range of behavioural, cognitive, personality and physiological variables.

Place among approaches. Because Zuckerman stresses the heritability of sensation seeking, his work falls into a different category from the behavioural and social-learning approaches, which emphasise situational factors and learning. This contrasts with Rotter, whose locus of control is presented as learned in childhood.

Commonsense appeal. The theory is intuitively appealing. It is easy to accept that people differ in their need for excitement, risk, change and adventure. Most of us know roughly how much of a sensation seeker we are, and we can judge friends and relatives fairly accurately from the activities they enjoy or avoid. Zuckerman's adjective study (Table 14.3) illustrates this: high sensation seekers described themselves as enthusiastic, playful, adventurous, elated, imaginative, daring, zany and mischievous; low sensation seekers as frightened, panicky, tense, nervous, shaky, fearful, worried and upset.

Highlights of research. The chapter summarises that high sensation seekers tend to score high in adventure seeking, disinhibition and boredom susceptibility; live in Westernised cultures; take risks, use drugs and alcohol, drive fast and have frequent sex; spend much time on computer games; be extraverted, open, conscientious and emotional; prefer helping professions to business; hold liberal political and religious views; be first-born or only children; and have more tattoos and piercings.

Evaluation points for a long answer. Strengths include a clear definition, a validated and widely translated scale, factor-analytically derived components, strong evidence for heritability and broad cross-cultural research. Limitations visible in the chapter include inconsistent findings (for example, computer misuse and birth order), the newer Need Inventory possibly being more reliable and valid than the original SSS, and evidence that environment shapes how the trait is expressed.
sections.simple: Sensation seeking research is still active and links the trait to behaviour, cognition, personality and physiology. Because Zuckerman stresses heredity, his work differs from learning-based theories, and the idea has commonsense appeal since we can easily judge our own and others' thrill-seeking.
keyPoints: Continues to stimulate research across behavioural, cognitive, personality and physiological variables.
Emphasis on heritability sets it apart from behavioural and social-learning approaches.
Commonsense appeal: people readily judge their own and others' sensation seeking.
Table 14.3: highs are enthusiastic, daring, playful; lows are fearful, tense, worried.
Weaknesses: some inconsistent findings (computer use, birth order).

sections.heading: Martin E. P. Seligman: Learned Helplessness and the Optimistic/Pessimistic Explanatory Style
sections.detailed:
In the mid-1960s Martin Seligman (born 1942) of the University of Pennsylvania, who would later lead the happiness and positive psychology movement, began research on a limited-domain facet of personality called learned helplessness. He first saw the phenomenon in a dog experiment on his very first day as a graduate student, and the chapter presents this moment as the start of both his own career direction and a new direction for psychology.

The original experiment had two parts. In the first part, dogs were classically conditioned to associate a high-pitched tone with an electric shock. This was a simple Pavlovian arrangement involving respondent behaviour: the tone was paired with the shock, and the dogs could do nothing about it.

In the second part, each dog was placed in a large box with two compartments separated by a low wall. A shock was delivered through the floor of the dog's compartment, and to escape it the dog had to perform an operant response: simply jump over the low barrier into the other, shock-free compartment. Dogs normally learn this quickly. The plan was then to test whether the tone alone, without shock, would produce the same jumping response, showing transfer from classical to operant conditioning.

The design therefore combined classical (respondent) and operant conditioning, and the key question was whether a fear learned in one situation would trigger escape behaviour in another. What actually happened, described in the next section, was unexpected and gave rise to the concept of learned helplessness.

Learned helplessness is defined in the glossary as a condition resulting from the perception that we have no control over our environment. Seligman later broadened this research to include optimism versus pessimism (explanatory style) and, later still, happiness and positive psychology, so this one accidental observation runs through the rest of the chapter.
sections.simple: In the mid-1960s, as a new graduate student at the University of Pennsylvania, Seligman saw a dog experiment that combined classical conditioning (tone paired with shock) and operant escape learning (jumping a barrier). It led him to the idea of learned helplessness: a condition that arises when we perceive we have no control over our environment.
keyPoints: Martin Seligman (1942-), University of Pennsylvania; began this research in the mid-1960s.
Saw the key experiment on his first day as a graduate student.
Part 1: Pavlovian conditioning of tone with unavoidable shock (respondent behaviour).
Part 2: shuttle box where jumping a low wall would escape shock (operant behaviour).
Learned helplessness: condition resulting from the perception of having no control over the environment.

sections.heading: A Shocking Finding
sections.detailed:
The experiment did not turn out as planned. When shock was delivered through the floor of their compartment, the dogs did not jump the barrier to escape. Instead they lay down, whimpered and made no effort to get away.

The experimenters were puzzled, but Seligman thought he understood. He proposed that during the first part of the experiment the dogs had learned that they were helpless: when the tone sounded there was nothing they could do to avoid the shock paired with it, so there was no point in trying. This learned expectation of futility apparently generalised to the second part of the experiment, even though an escape route was now available.

Seligman was struck by the implications. If dogs could learn something as complex as the futility of their own actions, this offered a laboratory analogy to human helplessness. He saw helplessness all around, in the urban poor, the newborn infant and the despondent patient who has given up. He wondered whether this could be a laboratory model that would explain how helplessness arises, how to cure and prevent it, which drugs might help, and who is especially vulnerable.

Determined to answer these questions, Seligman launched a research programme on learned helplessness, which he described as a condition resulting from the perception that we have no control over our environment and that nothing we do can change our situation. He later widened the programme to the issue of optimism versus pessimism and then to happiness.

For exam answers, the crucial insight is that the dogs' passivity was not caused by the shock itself but by what they had learned about the relationship between their responses and outcomes: that responding made no difference. This cognitive interpretation, an expectation that one's actions are futile, links learned helplessness to Rotter's external locus of control, and later to depression.
sections.simple: Instead of jumping to safety, the dogs lay down and whimpered. Seligman reasoned they had learned in part one that nothing they did mattered, and this expectation carried over even when escape was possible. He saw this as a model of human helplessness and started a research programme on it.
keyPoints: The dogs did not escape; they lay down, whimpered and gave up.
Seligman's explanation: they had learned in part one that their responses were futile.
The learned futility generalised to a situation where escape was possible.
Seligman saw a laboratory model for human helplessness (poor, infants, despondent patients).
Research later extended to optimism-pessimism and happiness.

sections.heading: Early Research
sections.detailed:
Studies with dogs. In Seligman's own early experiments, dogs were harnessed and given painful but not physically harmful shocks that they could not escape or avoid. They were then placed in a two-compartment shuttle box and shocked through the floor. Their behaviour was compared with that of a control group that had not received the earlier inescapable shocks.

Control dogs raced about until they happened to leap the barrier into the safe side, and on later trials they jumped faster each time, having learned how to escape. Experimental dogs ran around for about 30 seconds, then gave up, dropped to the floor and whimpered. They never learned to escape, even when the experimenters tried to lure them over the barrier with food. They had become passive and helpless (Overmier & Seligman, 1967; Seligman & Maier, 1967). The comparison with a control group shows that the helplessness came from prior uncontrollable experience, not from shock as such.

Studies with humans. Hiroto (1974) exposed an experimental group to a loud, irritating noise and told them they could turn it off by pressing buttons in the right sequence, but no correct sequence existed. A control group could stop the noise with an easy-to-learn sequence. Next, all subjects only had to move a hand from one side of a box to the other in response to a light to stop the noise. Control subjects learned this quickly; experimental subjects sat passively and made no attempt to deal with the noise.

Later research extended these findings. Learned helplessness occurred when people merely observed helpless models, especially models they saw as similar to themselves (Chamber & Hammonds, 2014); subjects seemed to reason that if the models could do nothing, neither could they. This shows that helplessness can be learned vicariously.

A meta-analysis of 132 studies with several thousand participants found that inescapable aversive stimulation affected humans even more strongly than animals. Learned helplessness has been documented in adult men and women, college students, adolescents, children, the elderly, unemployed women and psychiatric patients (Li, Mardhekar, & Wadkar, 2012; Villanova & Peterson, 1991).
