Everyday helplessness. Learned helplessness can occur in ordinary life whenever we face continuous intrusive stimuli we cannot control, such as noise from neighbours or outdoors, or being cyberbullied on social media (Evans & Stecker, 2004; Rabinowitz, 2005; Zucchi et al., 2012).
sections.simple: Dogs given inescapable shocks later gave up in a shuttle box after about 30 seconds and never learned to escape, unlike control dogs. Hiroto showed the same with people exposed to uncontrollable noise. People can also become helpless just by watching helpless models, the effect is stronger in humans than animals, and it happens in daily life with uncontrollable noise or cyberbullying.
keyPoints: Dogs pre-exposed to inescapable shock gave up after about 30 seconds; never learned to escape, even for food.
Control dogs learned to jump the barrier faster on each trial (Overmier & Seligman, 1967; Seligman & Maier, 1967).
Hiroto (1974): people exposed to unstoppable noise later failed to make a simple escape response.
Vicarious helplessness from observing similar helpless models (Chamber & Hammonds, 2014).
Meta-analysis of 132 studies: effects stronger in humans than animals; found in many groups and in everyday life.

sections.heading: Learned Helplessness as Torture
sections.detailed:
The techniques used in human and animal helplessness experiments were applied by the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and other organisations engaged in fighting terrorism. Prisoners were placed in situations where escape from painful stimuli was impossible.

The chapter gives examples: one prisoner was kept inside a coffin for days; another was waterboarded 83 times over 17 days; others were stripped and held in solitary confinement for days while extremely loud rock music was played continuously.

After such treatment the prisoners showed the same symptoms of learned helplessness as subjects in laboratory experiments. They became compliant and stopped trying to do anything about their conditions. This is exactly the passivity seen in Seligman's dogs and Hiroto's human subjects, which confirms how powerful uncontrollable aversive conditions can be.

When Seligman learned years later how his research had been used, he said he was grieved and horrified (McCoy, 2014).

This section is useful in exams for two reasons. It shows that the learned helplessness effect generalises far beyond the laboratory to extreme real-world conditions, and it raises an ethical point about how psychological findings can be misused for purposes their discoverers never intended.
sections.simple: The CIA and other anti-terrorism groups used helplessness methods on prisoners, such as confinement in a coffin, repeated waterboarding and loud music in solitary confinement. The prisoners became compliant and passive, just like the lab subjects, and Seligman was horrified when he learned of it.
keyPoints: Helplessness techniques were used by the CIA and other anti-terrorism organisations.
Examples: days in a coffin; waterboarding 83 times over 17 days; solitary confinement with deafening music.
Prisoners showed lab-style helplessness: compliant, stopped trying.
Seligman was 'grieved and horrified' (McCoy, 2014).
Illustrates real-world power and possible misuse of the research.

sections.heading: Learned Helplessness and Emotional Health
sections.detailed:
The benefits of having control over one's life for psychological health are widely documented, and this section presents the positive side of the helplessness research: perceived control protects emotional health, and it can be increased.

Cancer patients. Among cancer patients aged 29 to 80, those with the highest perception of control were better adjusted than patients who believed they had little control. This held even for severely debilitated patients. Patients who believed they could influence their illness, their recovery and their emotions showed better psychological adjustment than people in better physical condition who perceived little control (Thompson, Sobolew-Shubin, Galbraith, Schwankovsky, & Cruzen, 1993). The important point is that perceived control mattered more for adjustment than actual physical state.

Dental patients. People can also learn to feel more in control. Men and women averaging 55 years old who were scheduled for extensive dental work were first assessed for anxiety and desire for control in a dental setting. Half watched a stress inoculation training video; the control half watched a video about local sights. Patients who had low control but a strong desire for more control benefited most from the stress training video: during treatment they felt more in control and reported less pain than control-group patients (Law, Logan, & Baron, 1994).

These studies show that the opposite of learned helplessness, a sense of control, supports emotional adjustment, and that training can build it. This foreshadows Seligman's later programme of exercises to teach optimism and links to Rotter's finding that internals enjoy better mental health.
sections.simple: Feeling in control is good for mental health. Cancer patients who believed they had some control adjusted better, even if they were very ill, and dental patients who wanted more control felt more in control and less pain after watching a stress inoculation video.
keyPoints: Perceived control is widely linked to better psychological health.
Cancer patients (29-80) high in perceived control were better adjusted, even when severely debilitated (Thompson et al., 1993).
Perceived control mattered more than physical condition for adjustment.
Dental patients: stress inoculation training video increased feelings of control and reduced pain (Law et al., 1994).
Greatest benefit for those low in control but high in desire for control.

sections.heading: Animal Research on Learned Helplessness and Physical Health
sections.detailed:
Tumour rejection in rats. To test whether learned helplessness affects physical health, Seligman and colleagues injected rats with malignant tumour cells and assigned them to three conditions: escapable shock, inescapable shock or no shock (Visintainer, Volpicelli, & Seligman, 1982). Based on the number of cells injected, about half the rats would normally be expected to reject the tumour and survive.

The results were clear. In the no-shock control group, 50 percent rejected the tumour, as expected. In the escapable-shock group, who had some control, 70 percent rejected the tumour and survived. In the inescapable-shock (learned helplessness) group, only 27 percent rejected the malignant cells. The numbers 50, 70 and 27 are frequently asked. Notice that having control actually improved survival above the baseline, while helplessness reduced it.

Childhood experience. A similar study gave young rats the three conditions and later, as adults, injected them with malignant cells and exposed them to the same conditions. Most rats that had learned helplessness when young failed to reject the tumours as adults, whereas most rats that had learned control when young did reject them (Seligman & Visintainer, 1985). Seligman concluded that childhood experiences were crucial: early mastery 'immunized', while early helplessness put adult rats at risk for cancer.

Immune system. Learned helplessness was shown to weaken the immune system of rats (Maier, Laudenslager, & Ryan, 1985). The immune system includes T-cells and NK (natural killer) cells, which resist viruses, bacteria and tumour cells. In rats given inescapable shock, T-cells no longer multiplied rapidly in response to specific invaders, and NK cells lost their ability to destroy infections. This offers a possible physiological explanation for why helpless rats could not reject their tumours.

Sex differences. Later research found that most male rats exposed to uncontrollable stress never learned to escape, whereas most female rats did learn to escape. Learned helplessness was therefore easier to produce in males, suggesting that females may be less subject to the dangerous physiological changes found in the earlier work (Dalla, Edgecomb, Whetstone, & Shors, 2008).
sections.simple: Rats injected with tumour cells survived best with escapable shock (70 percent rejected the tumour), next with no shock (50 percent) and worst with inescapable shock (27 percent). Helplessness in youth made adult rats more vulnerable to cancer, helplessness weakened T-cells and NK cells, and helplessness was easier to produce in male than female rats.
keyPoints: Visintainer, Volpicelli & Seligman (1982): tumour rejection 70% escapable, 50% no shock, 27% inescapable.
Seligman & Visintainer (1985): early helplessness led to tumour failure in adulthood; early mastery protected.
Seligman: childhood mastery 'immunized'; early helplessness raised cancer risk.
Maier et al. (1985): helplessness weakened T-cells and NK cells.
Dalla et al. (2008): helplessness easier to establish in male than female rats.

sections.heading: Explanatory Style: Optimism and Pessimism
sections.detailed:
Seligman expanded his work on learned helplessness to include optimism versus pessimism. His key insight was that it is not only the lack of control in helplessness situations that affects us, but also how we explain that lack of control to ourselves. He proposed the concept of explanatory style to capture this.

Explanatory style is defined in the glossary as a way of explaining to ourselves our relative lack of control over the environment. An optimistic explanatory style can prevent learned helplessness, whereas a pessimistic explanatory style spreads helplessness to all facets of life.

In simple terms, optimists expect good things to happen to them and pessimists expect bad things to happen to them (Carver & Scheier, 2002). Leaning toward optimism or pessimism may shape many aspects of life. For example, optimists build better social networks and connections and are better able to cope with physical pain (Carver & Scheier, 2014; Ramirez-Maestre, Esteve, & Lopez, 2012), both valuable for dealing with life's challenges.

The attributional side of explanatory style is developed later in the chapter. Pessimists explain negative events in personal and pervasive terms, telling themselves that it is all their fault, that it will always be this way and that it will affect every part of their life (p. 393). The chapter summary (p. 404) formalises this as the attribution model of learned helplessness: failure is attributed to some cause, and pessimists attribute failures to internal, stable and global causes, while optimists attribute them to external, unstable and specific causes. In the summary's words, pessimists make personal, permanent and pervasive explanations, so helplessness changes from brief and localised to long-lasting and generalised.

To illustrate: after failing an exam, a pessimist might think 'I am stupid' (internal), 'I will always fail' (stable) and 'I mess up everything' (global). An optimist might think 'the paper was unusually hard' (external), 'this was one bad day' (unstable) and 'it is only this subject' (specific). The rest of the explanatory style material reports how these two styles relate to health, longevity, age, culture, stress, performance, cognition and depression, together with the downside of optimism.
sections.simple: Explanatory style is how we explain our lack of control to ourselves. Optimists expect good things and explain failures as external, temporary and specific, which protects them from helplessness. Pessimists expect bad things and explain failures as internal, permanent and pervasive, which spreads helplessness across life.
keyPoints: Explanatory style: how we explain our relative lack of control to ourselves.
Optimistic style prevents learned helplessness; pessimistic style spreads it to all facets of life.
Optimists expect good things, pessimists bad things (Carver & Scheier, 2002).
Optimists build better social networks and cope better with pain.
Attribution model (summary p. 404): pessimists = internal, stable, global; optimists = external, unstable, specific.

sections.heading: Explanatory Style and Physical Health and Longevity
sections.detailed:
Physical health. Seligman argues that optimists tend to be healthier than pessimists. Pessimists believe their actions make little difference, so they are less likely to prevent illness by changing smoking, diet and exercise habits or by seeking timely medical attention.

Young adult optimists were less likely to get sick, and when they did, they took more responsibility for their care, such as resting, seeing a doctor or drinking fluids (Peterson, Maier, & Seligman, 1993). Among college undergraduates, pessimists had twice as many infectious illnesses over a year as optimists. In Finland, optimists regained a positive attitude more quickly after the serious illness or death of a family member (Kivimaki et al., 2005). Optimists also cope better with health problems, recover faster from some medical procedures and manage stress better (Aspinwall & Tedeschi, 2010).

Cancer. Among breast cancer patients with a recurrence, optimists lived longer over five years, independent of illness severity. In Norway, breast cancer patients high in pessimism were far more anxious and depressed a year after treatment (Schou et al., 2004), and their optimism-pessimism levels stayed stable for the year regardless of prognosis (Schou et al., 2005). Optimistic breast cancer patients also function better socially and mentally and report higher quality of life (Colby & Shifren, 2013).

Heart and immunity. Optimists seem to develop stronger immune systems, recover more often from heart attacks and have less pain and fewer symptoms after heart surgery (Peterson & Seligman, 1987; Ronaldson et al., 2014). First-semester law students high in optimistic explanatory style had significantly more T-cells and NK cells (Segerstrom & Taylor, 1998). Adults aged 30 to 45 high in pessimism held more negative beliefs and had higher blood pressure (Räikkönen et al., 1999).

AIDS. Among homosexual and bisexual men, optimists had less psychological distress, fewer worries, believed they were at lower risk of AIDS and expected more control over the disease; HIV-positive men were more optimistic about not developing AIDS than HIV-negative men (Taylor et al., 1992). These beliefs may have been illusory, but they helped the men cope and reduced depression. The most optimistic men were no more likely to engage in high-risk sex, and in general the most optimistic took better care of their health.

Longevity. Nuns whose life stories written in their early 20s expressed optimism had a significantly lower death rate 60 years later (Danner, Snowdon, & Friesen, 2001). Among medical patients, optimists showed 19 percent greater longevity 30 years later (Maruta et al., 2002). Elderly optimists in England were in far better physical health (Steptoe et al., 2006).
sections.simple: Optimists get sick less, look after themselves better, recover faster, have stronger immune systems (more T-cells and NK cells) and lower blood pressure, and cope better with cancer, heart disease and HIV. They also live longer: optimistic nuns had lower death rates 60 years later, and optimistic patients lived 19 percent longer.
keyPoints: Pessimists think actions don't matter, so neglect prevention; pessimistic students had twice as many infectious illnesses.
Optimists recover faster from illness and family loss; optimistic breast cancer patients live longer and have better quality of life.
Optimists: stronger immunity (more T-cells and NK cells in law students), better heart recovery; pessimists: higher blood pressure.
HIV study (Taylor et al., 1992): optimism, even if illusory, reduced distress without increasing risky sex.
Longevity: nun study (60 years later) and 19% greater longevity after 30 years (Maruta et al., 2002).

sections.heading: Explanatory Style: Age, Culture and Stress
sections.detailed:
Age. People over 65 tend to have a more optimistic explanatory style and higher subjective well-being than younger people. Research on elderly people in China and the United States found that the more optimistic reported greater well-being and less depression (Hirsh et al., 2014; Isaacowitz, 2005a; Leung, Moneta, & McBride-Chang, 2005; Olson et al., 2014). A curious detail: elderly optimists tended to underreport their weight, while pessimists claimed to weigh more than they did (Sutin, 2013).

Culture. Black and Latina grandmothers who were primary caregivers for grandchildren, and Muslim college students in Kuwait and Oman, who were high in optimism were happier, had less depression, anxiety and hostility, and reported fewer sleep disorders than pessimists (Abdel-Khalek & Lester, 2010; Alansari & Kazem, 2008; Conway et al., 2008).

Cultural differences in explanatory style are well documented. American college students were more optimistic than Chinese-American students, who were more optimistic than mainland Chinese students (Lee & Seligman, 1997), the same acculturation gradient seen for locus of control. Kuwaiti students scored significantly lower on optimism than American students (Abdel-Khalek & Lester, 2006). Among Italian students, men were more optimistic than women (Colombo, Balbo, & Baruffi, 2006). Japanese students were more pessimistic than Americans: Americans predicted that positive events would happen to themselves rather than to others, while Japanese students thought positive events were more likely to happen to other people (Chang, Asakawa, & Sanna, 2001). The highlights box concludes that optimists tend to live in individualistic cultures.

Stress. Stressful life experience can lower optimism. Adults caring for a relative with Alzheimer's disease grew increasingly pessimistic over four years and experienced more anxiety, stress and physical complaints than non-caregivers (Robinson-Whelen et al., 1997). In the other direction, optimism protects against stress: college students higher in optimism at the start of their first semester had significantly less stress and depression during it (Brissette, Scheier, & Carver, 2002); optimistic middle-aged adults reported fewer depressive symptoms (Chang & Sanna, 2001); and the most optimistic third- to sixth-graders had fewer depressive symptoms and behaviour problems (Ey et al., 2005).
sections.simple: People over 65 tend to be more optimistic and happier. Optimists in many groups have less depression, anxiety and sleep trouble; Americans are more optimistic than Chinese Americans, who are more optimistic than mainland Chinese, and Japanese and Kuwaiti students are more pessimistic than Americans. Long-term stress like Alzheimer's caregiving increases pessimism, while optimism protects students, adults and children from stress and depression.
keyPoints: Over-65s: more optimistic, higher well-being; elderly optimists underreport weight (Sutin, 2013).
Optimistic caregiver grandmothers and Muslim students in Kuwait and Oman: happier, less depression, anxiety, hostility, fewer sleep disorders.
Lee & Seligman (1997): Americans > Chinese Americans > mainland Chinese in optimism.
Kuwaiti and Japanese students more pessimistic than Americans; Italian men more optimistic than women.
Alzheimer's caregivers grew more pessimistic over 4 years; optimism predicts less stress and depression in students, adults and children.

sections.heading: Explanatory Style: Performance, Cognitive Functioning and the Downside of Optimism
sections.detailed:
Performance. American college optimists typically earned better grades than pessimists, and the same was found in Kuwait (El-Anzi, 2005). When pessimists received lower grades than their peers, they were more depressed about it than optimists with similarly low grades (Gibbons et al., 2000). In France, 14- to 16-year-olds who were led to believe they had failed a basketball dribbling contest responded differently depending on explanatory style: those high in optimism were less anxious, more confident and performed better on a second test than those high in pessimism (Martin-Krumm, Sarrazin, Peterson, & Famose, 2003).

Cognitive functioning. Optimism and pessimism also influence thinking. Pessimistic college students were more likely to attend to negative stimuli, while optimistic students attended to both positive and negative stimuli (Segerstrom, 2001). This is a subtle point: optimists do not ignore bad information, they simply do not focus on it exclusively. In Germany, optimistic students were flexible and adaptable in their cognitive activities, while pessimists were more often inflexible, rigid and likely to give up on goals (Weber, Vollmann, & Renner, 2007).

The downside of optimism. Optimism is not always beneficial (Schneider, 2001). Some optimists hold unrealistic views about their vulnerability, so they may drink or use drugs to excess, believing their positive attitude protects them despite contrary evidence. Highly optimistic students who expected to do well on an exam felt more disappointed when they got their scores than less optimistic students (Sweeny & Shepperd, 2010). Students gambling at a casino near their university showed that optimists kept gambling despite consistent losses, while pessimists were more likely to stop, because optimists kept expecting to win (Gibson & Sanbonmatsu, 2004).

This unrealistic optimism, the belief that good things are much more likely to happen to oneself than to others, is more common in individualistic cultures such as the United States than in collectivist cultures such as China, and more common in men than women (Lin & Raghubir, 2005).

Unrealistic pessimism. The opposite extreme is also harmful. Unrealistic pessimism in adversity, such as a serious illness, means telling yourself you will never cope or overcome the situation, which also shows low self-efficacy. It can lead to lack of effort and therefore lack of success (Blanton, Axsom, McClive, & Price, 2001). A balanced answer should therefore say that realistic optimism is most adaptive.
sections.simple: Optimists get better grades, take setbacks less hard and perform better after failure. They notice both good and bad information and think more flexibly, while pessimists focus on the negative and give up. But unrealistic optimism can lead to excess drinking, bigger disappointment and continued gambling despite losses, and unrealistic pessimism can stop people trying at all.
keyPoints: Optimists earn better grades (US, Kuwait); pessimists more depressed by low grades.
French teen athletes high in optimism performed better after supposed failure.
Pessimists attend to negative stimuli; optimists attend to both (Segerstrom, 2001); optimists more cognitively flexible.
Downside: unrealistic optimism linked to excess drinking/drugs, bigger exam disappointment, continued gambling despite losses.
Unrealistic optimism more common in individualistic cultures and men; unrealistic pessimism reduces effort and success.

sections.heading: Pessimism and Depression; the Attributional Model
sections.detailed:
Helplessness and depression. Seligman found a strong association between learned helplessness and depression. A major symptom of depression is the feeling of being unable to control life events, and Seligman called depression the 'ultimate pessimism'. Severely depressed people believe they are helpless and see little point in trying, because they expect nothing to turn out well.

Table 14.4 sets out the parallels between learned helplessness (in animals) and depression: passivity in both; difficulty learning that responses produce relief versus difficulty learning that responses produce outcomes; lack of aggression versus introjected hostility; weight loss and anorexia versus loss of libido; norepinephrine depletion in both; and ulcers and stress in both, with feelings of helplessness in depression. Norepinephrine is a neurotransmitter, and severe depression is associated with its deficiency, which can lower energy and deepen depression.

Depression and the body. Depression also increases risk of physical illness by reducing immune effectiveness, suppressing NK cell activity and altering white blood cell count, findings confirmed by more than 40 studies over ten years (Herbert & Cohen, 1993; Weisse, 1992).

Why some people recover. Everyone feels helpless sometimes, after failure or under family or job pressure, and most people recover. Some, however, generalise failure in one area, such as a poor grade or a missed promotion, to other areas of life and to their sense of self-worth, becoming helpless and depressed in all situations. According to Seligman, the difference lies in explanatory style. A pessimistic style turns learned helplessness from brief and local into long-lasting and general; helplessness becomes full-blown depression when the person who fails is a pessimist, whereas in optimists failure brings only brief demoralisation. Pessimists explain negative events in personal and pervasive terms, such as 'It's all my fault', 'It's always going to be this way' and 'It's going to affect every aspect of my life'.

The attributional model. The chapter summary (p. 404) names this the attribution model of learned helplessness. Pessimists attribute failure to internal (personal), stable (permanent) and global (pervasive) causes; optimists attribute failure to external, unstable and specific causes.

Supporting research. At the start of a semester, undergraduates were tested for explanatory style and asked what grade would count as personal failure. After the midterm, among students who got a 'failure' grade, 30 percent of optimists but 70 percent of pessimists showed symptoms of depression. Similar results were found with other college students and with third-graders: explanatory style predicted depression (Nolen-Hoeksema, Girgus, & Seligman, 1987; Zullow & Seligman, 1985). Research in the United States and Finland found that people high in pessimism were more likely to take antidepressants and to be at risk for suicide (Chang et al., 2013; Kronstrom et al., 2014).
sections.simple: Seligman linked helplessness to depression, which he called the 'ultimate pessimism', and the symptoms of the two closely match. Whether a failure leads to lasting depression depends on explanatory style: pessimists blame internal, permanent, pervasive causes, so 70 percent of pessimistic students who got a 'failure' grade became depressed, compared with 30 percent of optimists.
keyPoints: Depression = 'ultimate pessimism'; main symptom is feeling unable to control events.
Table 14.4: shared passivity, norepinephrine depletion, ulcers and stress; depression weakens immunity (NK cells).
Pessimistic style turns brief, local helplessness into long-lasting, general depression.
Attribution model: pessimists = internal, stable, global (personal, permanent, pervasive); optimists = external, unstable, specific.
Grade study: 70% of pessimists vs 30% of optimists became depressed after a 'failure' grade; pessimists more at risk for antidepressant use and suicide.

sections.heading: The Development of Learned Helplessness in Childhood
sections.detailed:
Although learned helplessness can occur at any age, Seligman suggested that we are particularly vulnerable to it in infancy and early childhood, and that helplessness experienced in these formative years can predispose a person to a pessimistic explanatory style (Seligman, 1975).

Response-outcome learning. Infants begin life totally helpless, with no control over their environment. As they mature they gain control: crying brings caregivers, and crawling, walking and talking each bring new possibilities for control, and for failure. Through these early interactions with the physical and social environment, a child's sense of helplessness or of mastery and control is established. When an infant responds, the response may change the environment (bringing food, a toy or a hug) or may have no effect. At a primitive level infants form associations between responses and outcomes. If responses do not lead to successful outcomes, the result is learned helplessness: infants learn that particular responses do not work and may generalise this to believe that no response will work, producing a general sense of having no control over life. A high correlation between responses and outcomes, by contrast, gives positive feedback that builds mastery and control.

Parents and heredity. A consistent explanatory style develops by about age 8 and is strongly influenced by the parents' explanatory style; Seligman wrote that pessimistic parents have pessimistic children. Studies in India found that children's optimism is strongly influenced by parents' level of education: the more formal education parents have, the more optimistic their children (Daraei & Ghaderi, 2012). Research with adolescents in the Netherlands and other countries also found that attributional style is influenced both by learning and by genetic factors (Lau, Rijsdijk, & Eley, 2006; Mavioglu, Boomsma, & Bartels, 2015).

Later childhood. Helplessness may also develop later in childhood from bullying by peers, a harsh school environment or other negative experiences, and race and poverty are related to it. Students who often conflict with peers and are treated by classmates and teachers as less intelligent or skilled may develop learned helplessness (Orejudo et al., 2012). Low social support from parents and family can lead to high pessimism in children (Ciarrochi & Heaven, 2008).

The chapter summary (p. 404) adds that the major causes of learned helplessness are maternal deprivation and an environment providing low levels of stimulation and feedback.
sections.simple: Babies start out helpless and learn whether their actions (crying, crawling, talking) produce results; if they don't, they learn helplessness and may generalise it. A stable explanatory style forms by about age 8 and mirrors the parents' style, though genes play a role too; bullying, harsh schools, poverty, race and low family support can also create helplessness, and the summary names maternal deprivation and low stimulation as major causes.
keyPoints: Infancy and early childhood are especially vulnerable periods (Seligman, 1975).
Infants learn response-outcome links; responses that bring no outcome produce generalised helplessness.
Consistent explanatory style by about age 8, shaped by parents' style; 'pessimistic parents also have pessimistic children'.
India: more parental education = more optimistic children; Netherlands: learning and genes both matter.
Later causes: bullying, harsh schools, race, poverty, being treated as less able, low family support; summary: maternal deprivation and low stimulation and feedback.

sections.heading: Reflections on Learned Helplessness
sections.detailed:
The concepts of learned helplessness and optimism versus pessimism have generated hundreds of research studies. Seligman and his colleagues have applied them to sports, politics, religion, child rearing and job performance, and overall a large and impressive body of data supports the learned helplessness concept.

Applications. Seligman designed a programme of exercises to teach optimism to adults and children, moving his findings out of the laboratory and into the home and workplace. This practical step follows from the evidence that explanatory style is partly learned and that perceived control can be increased (as in the dental stress inoculation study).

Extension to positive psychology. Seligman later extended his ideas to positive psychology and the factors that influence subjective well-being, in other words the question 'What makes us happy?'. This shift from studying helplessness and depression to studying happiness and flourishing is one of the defining features of his career.

Highlights of research on optimism. The chapter summarises that people high in optimism tend to get sick less often and experience less stress and depression; live longer; recover faster from the death of a family member; live in individualistic cultures such as the United States rather than collectivist ones; earn better grades; be more flexible and adaptable in their thinking; and even dribble a basketball better.

Evaluation points. Strengths include rigorous experimental work with animals and humans, a clear link between laboratory findings and real problems such as depression and illness, and a wide range of applications. Points to mention critically, drawn from the chapter, are that some animal findings (such as tumour rejection) may not translate directly to humans, that optimism has a downside when unrealistic, that results differ across cultures, and that the techniques have been misused for torture.
sections.simple: Hundreds of studies support learned helplessness and the optimism-pessimism idea, applied to sport, politics, religion, parenting and work. Seligman created exercises to teach optimism and then moved on to positive psychology and the question of what makes people happy.
keyPoints: Hundreds of studies; large, impressive supporting data.
Applied to sports, politics, religion, child rearing and job performance.
Seligman developed exercises to teach optimism to adults and children.
Extended to positive psychology and subjective well-being: 'What makes us happy?'
Highlights: optimists are healthier, live longer, get better grades, think more flexibly.

sections.heading: Martin Seligman: Positive Psychology
sections.detailed:
Seligman advanced positive psychology in the late 1990s during his term as president of the American Psychological Association. His argument was that psychology should deal not only with problems such as helplessness and depression but with the best of human functioning: happiness, excellence and optimal human growth.

The move is a natural continuation of his earlier work. Learned helplessness showed how people come to give up; explanatory style showed how optimism protects against helplessness; positive psychology asks what makes people flourish and be happy. The chapter frames this as the question 'What makes us happy?'.

Before reviewing the research, the chapter does something unusual: it examines Seligman's own life to see whether he meets his own criteria for happiness, or subjective well-being. The answer, given in the next section, is surprising and introduces the idea that there are different kinds of happiness.

Comparison with humanistic psychology. One review question asks how Seligman's positive psychology compares with the earlier humanistic psychology of Maslow and Rogers. From the chapter, the clear similarity is the shared focus on the positive side of human nature: optimal growth, excellence and fulfilment rather than pathology. The difference visible in this chapter is method and emphasis: Seligman's positive psychology rests on a very large body of empirical research using measures of subjective well-being, life satisfaction, optimism and personality across many countries, and it identifies measurable correlates of happiness, whereas the chapter presents positive psychology as an empirical research field with its own journals. Students should draw on the earlier chapters on Maslow and Rogers for the humanistic side of this comparison.
sections.simple: In the late 1990s, as APA president, Seligman launched positive psychology: the study of the best in people, such as happiness, excellence and optimal growth. It grew out of his work on helplessness and optimism and asks what makes people happy.
keyPoints: Advanced by Seligman in the late 1990s as APA president.
Focus: best of human functioning - happiness, excellence, optimal growth.
Continuation of learned helplessness and optimism research.
Central question: 'What makes us happy?'
Shares humanistic psychology's positive focus but is strongly research-based.

sections.heading: The Life of Seligman (1942-)
sections.detailed:
Seligman's writings suggest that he is not especially happy himself. Despite his success and celebrity, he admitted that he is rarely happy in the sense of feeling joyful. In 2010 he placed himself among the lowest 30 percent of people for positive feelings and emotions. He told a reporter that a life can be good and satisfying without positive feeling, and that his own life now revolves around meaning and purpose. Earlier, in a study of students in the top 10 percent of happiness, he said he would not have qualified for that group (Diener & Seligman, 2002).

He added, however, that there are different kinds of happiness and that he is one of those who find their deepest satisfaction in being fully engaged in work; his wife agreed that he is happiest then. This anticipates his later distinction between the pleasant, engaged and meaningful lives.

When Seligman was 13 his father suffered a severe stroke that left him disabled and almost helpless. Seligman said the experience left his emotions 'frozen over' and cast an important shadow over his life. Students may note the link between witnessing a parent's helplessness and his later research topic, though the chapter does not state this connection directly.

He attended a private prep school in Albany, New York, where most students came from wealthy upper-class families. He felt like an outsider, aware of the differences between himself and the others, and isolated and alone; a close friend believed he never fully lost that feeling and might still struggle inwardly with acceptance. Even so, his intelligence and hard work took him to Princeton and to a Ph.D. at the University of Pennsylvania in 1967. He is director of the university's Positive Psychology Center and a champion bridge player who has won several tournaments.
sections.simple: Seligman says he is rarely joyful and ranks himself in the lowest 30 percent for positive emotion, finding satisfaction instead in meaning and engagement with work. His father's stroke when he was 13 deeply affected him, and he felt like an outsider at a wealthy prep school, but he went on to Princeton, a Penn Ph.D. (1967) and directing the Positive Psychology Center.
keyPoints: Rarely feels joyful; in 2010 ranked himself in lowest 30% for positive emotions.
Finds satisfaction in meaning, purpose and full engagement in work.
Father's severe stroke when Seligman was 13 left his emotions 'frozen over'.
Felt an isolated outsider at an elite Albany prep school.
Princeton; Ph.D. University of Pennsylvania 1967; director of Positive Psychology Center; champion bridge player.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Causes of Happiness
sections.detailed:
Positive psychology asks what the happy personality looks like and how happy people differ from those who are not happy. Psychologists have labelled the happy personality with terms such as subjective well-being or life satisfaction.

Subjective well-being is defined as encompassing two parts: a cognitive evaluation of the quality of one's life experience, and the possession of positive moods and emotions. Happiness therefore has both a rational aspect (judging one's life as satisfying) and an emotional aspect (feeling good). This two-part definition is worth quoting in any answer on positive psychology, because some later findings separate the two; for example, higher income raises life satisfaction more than it raises happiness.

Research has identified many factors that can influence happiness, and the chapter reviews them one by one: money, physical attractiveness, health, age (including adolescence and older people), marriage and social support, culture, geography, race and ethnicity, personality, self-efficacy and internal locus of control, thinking positively, goals, the relationship between happiness and success, and Internet use.

A useful way to organise these for a 10-mark answer is into external circumstances (money, attractiveness, health, age, marriage, culture, geography, ethnicity, Internet) and internal or psychological factors (personality traits, control beliefs, positive emotions, gratitude, goals). The chapter's overall message is that many external circumstances act as necessary but not sufficient conditions, while personality and outlook are among the strongest predictors.

The highlights box lists that happy people tend to: have more money and live in a wealthy country; be more attractive; exercise more as they get older; be married and without children; have a strong ethnic identity; be extraverted, conscientious and high in self-efficacy and internal control; not be neurotic; be enthusiastic, optimistic and grateful; have goals, a healthy lifestyle and social involvement; balance personal life and work; and spend time on the Internet, or maybe not.
sections.simple: Happiness is studied as subjective well-being or life satisfaction, which combines a thoughtful judgement that your life is good with positive moods and emotions. Researchers have looked at many influences, from money and health to personality and goals.
keyPoints: Happy personality = subjective well-being or life satisfaction.
Two parts: cognitive evaluation of life quality + positive moods and emotions.
Happiness has rational and emotional aspects.
Factors reviewed: money, attractiveness, health, age, marriage, culture, geography, ethnicity, personality, control, positive thinking, goals, success, Internet.
Many circumstances are necessary but not sufficient; personality is a strong predictor.

sections.heading: Money
sections.detailed:
The chapter confirms the old saying that money does not buy happiness, but adds that lack of money can cause unhappiness. An income adequate for basic needs is a necessary but not sufficient condition for happiness.

Studies in Sweden, Turkey and other European countries found the lowest happiness in low-income households, and a major source of satisfaction was having a cash reserve for minor emergencies (Berlin & Kaunitz, 2014; Drakopoulos & Grimani, 2013). A survey in 123 nations confirmed that life satisfaction varies with income: people who earn more report being more satisfied, though not necessarily happier (Diener, Ng, Harter, & Arora, 2010). This shows the value of separating the cognitive and emotional parts of well-being. Money may be mentioned as important for happiness more often by Americans than by Europeans (Mogilner, 2010).

People who cannot afford essentials are unhappy, but money well beyond what is needed has little measurable effect. Even a large lottery win usually produces only a temporary increase in subjective well-being (DeNeve & Cooper, 1998; Diener et al., 1999; King & Napa, 1998; Pappas, 2010).

More and costlier possessions do not guarantee happiness. Van Boven (2005) concluded that the more people endorse materialistic goals, the less happy and satisfied they are. High-income people also tend to experience more stress and spend less time on relaxation and leisure than people with lower incomes (Kahneman et al., 2006).

Summary for exams: poverty lowers happiness; adequate income and an emergency cushion matter; extra wealth raises life satisfaction somewhat but not happiness much; lottery gains fade; materialism and the stress of high-income life work against well-being.
sections.simple: Money can't buy happiness, but not having enough for basic needs makes people unhappy. Earning more raises life satisfaction but not necessarily happiness, lottery wins give only a temporary boost, materialistic people are less happy, and high earners have more stress and less leisure.
keyPoints: Adequate income is necessary but not sufficient for happiness.
Lowest happiness in low-income households; a cash reserve for emergencies is a key satisfaction.
123-nation survey: higher income = more satisfied, not necessarily happier (Diener et al., 2010).
Money beyond needs has little effect; lottery wins give temporary gains.
Materialism lowers happiness (Van Boven, 2005); high earners have more stress and less leisure.

sections.heading: Physical Attractiveness
sections.detailed:
Are attractive people happier? Research in the United States, Canada, England and Germany says yes: personal attractiveness does seem to increase happiness. However, the chapter suggests an indirect explanation. Physical attractiveness generally improves marriage prospects, job opportunities and income potential (Anderson, Adams, & Plaut, 2008; Bennett, 2011; Hamermesh & Abrevaya, 2011), and these advantages, rather than looks themselves, may raise happiness.

The link between attractiveness and happiness is stronger for people living in cities than for those in rural areas, perhaps because appearance plays a larger role in urban social and economic life.

Research in Finland also found that people who appear obese are less happy than those who are not obese (Bockerman, Johansson, Saarni, & Saarni, 2014).

For an answer on the effect of attractiveness (part of a review question), the key points are: a positive relationship exists in several Western countries; it may operate through marriage, jobs and income; it is stronger in urban settings; and visible obesity is associated with lower happiness.
sections.simple: Attractive people tend to be happier, probably because good looks help with marriage, jobs and income. The link is stronger in cities than rural areas, and in Finland people who look obese are less happy.
keyPoints: Attractiveness increases happiness (US, Canada, England, Germany).
Likely indirect: better marriage prospects, jobs and income.
Stronger relationship in cities than rural areas.
Finland: people who appear obese are less happy (Bockerman et al., 2014).

sections.heading: Health
sections.detailed:
Health relates to happiness in an asymmetric way. Poor health can diminish happiness, but good health does not guarantee it, so health appears to be a necessary but not sufficient condition for subjective well-being, the same pattern as money.

The relationship also runs the other way, and more strongly. Being happy contributes to health and longer life. A review of more than 160 studies confirmed that high subjective well-being contributes to greater longevity and better health (Diener & Chan, 2011).

Exercise is one link. A survey of 25 countries found that people who exercise actively report higher life satisfaction than those who do not (Dolan, Kavetsos, & Vlaev, 2014). Later sections add that both aerobic and strength exercise correlate strongly with happiness in older people.

Connections with the rest of the chapter: optimists and internals are also physically healthier, and the chapter summary says happy people tend to be in better health and live longer. An answer on the effect of health (part of a review question) should stress the two directions: health is necessary but not sufficient for happiness, while happiness actively promotes health and longevity.
sections.simple: Being unhealthy can make you unhappy, but being healthy doesn't guarantee happiness. Happiness, though, helps health: a review of over 160 studies found happy people live longer and are healthier, and people who exercise report higher life satisfaction.
keyPoints: Health is necessary but not sufficient for subjective well-being.
Happiness contributes to better health and longevity (review of 160+ studies, Diener & Chan, 2011).
25-country survey: exercisers report higher life satisfaction (Dolan et al., 2014).
Effect runs both ways but happiness-to-health is emphasised.

sections.heading: Age and Adolescence
sections.detailed:
Age. A survey of more than 300,000 Americans aged 18 to 85 found that subjective well-being and life satisfaction were high at 18, declined until about age 50, and then rose so that 85-year-olds reported greater life satisfaction than 18-year-olds (Stone, Schwartz, Broderick, & Deaton, 2010). This U-shaped pattern has not been duplicated everywhere. A worldwide Gallup survey found that in English-speaking developed nations of Western Europe, well-being dropped between 45 and 54, while in less developed nations of Eastern Europe, the former Soviet Union and Latin America happiness declined overall with age (Steptoe, Deaton, & Stone, 2015). So the age pattern depends on national context.

Adolescence. American adolescents high in subjective well-being are far more likely to have parents who value them, show interest in them and care about their future; this link appears stronger for girls than boys (Rayle, 2005). Happier American adolescents had more positive peer relationships, less anxiety and depression, greater hopes for the future, and a stronger feeling of personal control over their lives (Gilman & Huebner, 2006), which connects happiness to Rotter's internal control.

In China, teenagers high in subjective well-being had better-educated parents who rarely quarrelled (Guo-Xing & Hai, 2006). In Israel, adolescents who felt strong social support from the community and friends were happier than those who felt little support (Ronen et al., 2014).

The adolescent findings point to family warmth and interest, parental harmony and education, peer relationships, social support and a sense of control as sources of young people's happiness.
sections.simple: In the US, happiness is high at 18, dips to around 50 and then rises, so 85-year-olds are more satisfied than 18-year-olds, but other countries show different patterns. Happy teenagers have caring, interested, educated parents who don't fight, good friends, social support and a sense of control.
keyPoints: 300,000+ Americans: well-being high at 18, lowest around 50, higher at 85 than 18 (Stone et al., 2010).
Gallup: Western Europe dip at 45-54; Eastern Europe, former USSR, Latin America decline with age.
Happy US teens have parents who value them (stronger for girls); positive peers, low anxiety, sense of control.
China: happy teens have educated, rarely quarrelling parents.
Israel: community and friend support makes adolescents happier.

sections.heading: Older People
sections.detailed:
Studies of older people suggest that happiness does not necessarily fall with advancing age, but the findings are inconsistent: some show increasing happiness with age, while others suggest happiness peaks at 65 and then declines (Lacey, Smith, & Ubel, 2006; Mroczek & Spiro, 2005).

Health and attitude. In Germany, adults aged 70 to 103 who had health problems and physical limitations suffered a decline in subjective well-being (Kunzmann, Little, & Smith, 2000). Yet another German study of older hospitalised patients with disabilities found that it was not the impairments themselves so much as the person's attitude toward them that lowered well-being; those with more positive attitudes were happier (Schneider et al., 2006). In Slovakia, elderly people high in 'a belief in a just world' reported more happiness than those without this belief (Dzuka & Dalbert, 2006). Attitude therefore moderates the effect of physical decline.

Exercise and social networks. Both aerobic exercise and resistance or strength training correlate strongly and positively with happiness in the elderly (Netz, Wu, Becker, & Tenanbaum, 2005). Older people with stronger social networks and supportive friends report more happiness than socially isolated people (Pinquart & Soerensen, 2000).

Impending death. Studies of people aged 70 to 100 in the United States, England and Germany found that approaching death contributes to a decline in well-being; the last three to five years of life are often marked by a rapid fall in reported happiness (Gerstorf et al., 2008, 2010).

Exam summary: happiness in old age depends less on age itself than on health, attitude, beliefs, exercise and social support, with a terminal decline in the last few years of life.
sections.simple: Happiness doesn't necessarily drop in old age, though findings vary. Health problems reduce well-being, but a positive attitude matters more than the disability itself; belief in a just world, exercise and supportive friends raise happiness, while the last three to five years of life bring a sharp decline.
keyPoints: Findings inconsistent: some show rising happiness, others a peak at 65 then decline.
Health problems lower well-being (Germany, 70-103), but attitude toward infirmity matters more (Schneider et al., 2006).
Belief in a just world linked to happiness in elderly Slovaks.
Aerobic and strength exercise and strong social networks raise happiness.
Rapid decline in happiness in the last 3-5 years of life (Gerstorf et al.).

sections.heading: Marriage and Social Support
sections.detailed:
Marriage. Research in more than 40 countries with about 60,000 people shows clearly that married people report higher happiness than those who are divorced, separated, widowed or never married (Carr et al., 2014; Diener, Gohm, Suh, & Oishi, 2000). Married women of all ages are happier than unmarried women, and married men are happier than unmarried men, in countries including the United States and Poland.

Children. Happiness declines for both husbands and wives after the birth of their first child. In general, people without children report greater happiness than parents, and those with very young children report the least (Munsey, 2010). The lowest happiness of all has been found among unmarried mothers as a group (Ifcher & Zarghamee, 2014).

Spouses and divorce. A 35-year longitudinal study of married couples found that each partner's happiness varies with the other's: unhappiness in one spouse often leads to unhappiness in the other, and the converse is true (Hoppmann et al., 2011). In Germany, people who go through more than one divorce score higher in life satisfaction after the second divorce than after the first (Luhmann & Eid, 2009).

Social support. Social support correlates highly with subjective well-being in most countries. In Israel, life satisfaction was higher among people with strong support networks, especially new immigrants (Litwin, 2005). In Finland, active social support was critical to recent immigrants' psychological well-being (Jasinskaja-Lahti et al., 2006). The next section shows an important cultural exception in collectivist societies.
sections.simple: Married people are happier than single, divorced or widowed people across 40+ countries. But having children lowers happiness, especially very young kids, and unmarried mothers are least happy; spouses' happiness rises and falls together. Social support strongly predicts well-being, especially for immigrants.
keyPoints: 40+ countries, ~60,000 people: married people happier than divorced, separated, widowed or never married.
Happiness declines after first child; childless people happier; very young children = least happy; unmarried mothers lowest.
35-year study: spouses' happiness moves together (Hoppmann et al., 2011).
Germany: more satisfied after second divorce than after first.
Social support predicts well-being, especially for immigrants (Israel, Finland).

sections.heading: Culture
sections.detailed:
Denmark consistently ranks highest in all major international happiness surveys (Hussain, 2014). Happiness varies across cultures, and a nation's relative wealth is of major importance. Countries so poor that basic needs are hard to satisfy have much lower happiness than economically advanced countries, and people in wealthier countries rate themselves happier than those in impoverished ones (Diener, Diener, & Diener, 1995; Veenhoven, 2005; and others).

Social support in collectivist cultures. Studies in collectivist Eastern cultures such as China and Turkey found little relationship between social support and subjective well-being (Dan, Jun, & Ji-Liang, 2006; Turkum, 2005). Turkish college students' well-being was significantly related to the chance to give support to others, but receiving support had no effect (Gencoz & Ozlale, 2004). This contrasts with the strong support-happiness link in most countries.

Individualism. Subjective well-being is markedly higher in individualistic cultures such as the United States than in collectivist cultures such as China (Diener, Suh, Smith, & Shao, 1995; Park & Huebner, 2005; Wirtz et al., 2009), consistent with the findings on optimism and internal control.

Cultural inheritance. Descendants of immigrants tend to reflect the well-being typical of their ancestral culture even without continued contact. Danes and Swedes report high well-being, as do Americans with ancestors from those countries; Americans whose ancestors came from lower well-being cultures such as Hungary and Lithuania have similarly lower well-being (Rice & Steele, 2004).

For a review question on culture: wealth, individualism and ancestral culture all relate to national happiness, and the role of social support differs in collectivist societies.
sections.simple: Denmark always ranks happiest. Wealthy and individualistic countries are happier than poor and collectivist ones. In China and Turkey, receiving social support doesn't predict happiness much, though giving it does in Turkey, and descendants of immigrants keep the happiness level of their ancestors' culture.
keyPoints: Denmark ranks highest in all major international happiness surveys.
National wealth is a major factor; poor countries much less happy.
China and Turkey: little link between social support and well-being; in Turkey giving, not receiving, support matters.
Individualistic cultures (US) happier than collectivist ones (China).
Immigrants' descendants reflect ancestral culture's well-being (Denmark, Sweden high; Hungary, Lithuania low).

sections.heading: Geography: Where You Live Is Important
sections.detailed:
A nationwide survey of Americans aged 25 to 75 found that the criteria for happiness differ in various parts of the United States (Plaut, Markus, & Lachman, 2002).

People in the New England states considered physical well-being, autonomy and not feeling constrained necessary for subjective well-being. People in the western south-central states (Texas, Oklahoma, Arkansas and Louisiana) were more concerned with personal growth and with feelings of cheerfulness and happiness. People in the eastern south-central states (Kentucky, Tennessee, Mississippi and Alabama) focused more on social responsibility and contributing to the welfare of others as necessary for their own happiness.

Other research found that subjective well-being was highest in the west coast and mountain states, moderately high in the east coast states and lowest in the midwestern and southern states. Overall, happiness was significantly related to higher income, more education and greater tolerance for other people's views (Rentfrow, Mellander, & Florida, 2009).

A study in regions of Germany over 24 years found that as people aged, life satisfaction remained higher among those living in affluent areas than among those in less affluent regions (Gerstorf et al., 2010).

The lesson is that both what people mean by happiness and how happy they are vary by region, and regional wealth, education and tolerance help explain the differences.
sections.simple: Different US regions define happiness differently: New Englanders value health and autonomy, western south-central residents value growth and cheerfulness, and eastern south-central residents value helping others. Happiness is highest on the west coast and mountain states and lowest in the Midwest and South, linked to income, education and tolerance; in Germany, affluent regions stay happier as people age.
keyPoints: Plaut et al. (2002): criteria for happiness differ by US region.
New England: physical well-being, autonomy, not feeling constrained.
Western south-central: personal growth, cheerfulness; eastern south-central: social responsibility.
Well-being highest in west coast/mountain states, lowest in Midwest and South; linked to income, education, tolerance.
Germany (24 years): affluent regions keep higher life satisfaction with age.

sections.heading: Race and Ethnicity
sections.detailed:
Ethnic identity. In multicultural societies, people with a stronger sense of ethnic identity rate higher in subjective well-being than people who identify weakly with their ethnic heritage (Le, Lai, & Wallen, 2009). African-American college students who felt more identified with and accepted by the Black community at their college reported higher psychological well-being (Postmes & Branscombe, 2002).

Discrimination. African-American adults who had experienced discrimination reported lower life satisfaction than those who had not. Those who had attended predominantly White schools reported higher life satisfaction than those from predominantly Black or mixed-race schools, though the chapter cautions this may have changed in the decades since the research (Broman, 1997).

Older African Americans (aged 55 to 93) who reported stress from racial discrimination had lower life satisfaction (Utsey, Payne, Jackson, & Jones, 2002). Similarly, Black college students who perceived more racial discrimination had lower life satisfaction and more symptoms of depression (Prelow, Mosher, & Bowman, 2006; Seaton & Yip, 2009).

The chapter summary condenses this as: high subjective well-being is associated with not being a member of a minority group that experiences discrimination. A balanced answer should mention both the protective effect of strong ethnic identity and acceptance and the damaging effect of discrimination.
sections.simple: A strong sense of ethnic identity and acceptance by one's own community goes with greater well-being. Experiencing racial discrimination lowers life satisfaction and increases depression among African Americans of all ages.
keyPoints: Stronger ethnic identity = higher subjective well-being (Le et al., 2009).
African-American students accepted by the Black campus community had higher well-being.
Discrimination lowers life satisfaction in African-American adults (Broman, 1997) and older adults (Utsey et al., 2002).
Black college students perceiving discrimination: lower life satisfaction, more depression.
Broman: predominantly White school attendees more satisfied, possibly dated.

sections.heading: Personality
sections.detailed:
Big Five. Much research has examined the personality correlates of happiness, especially the five-factor model. People low in neuroticism and high in extraversion, agreeableness and conscientiousness report high subjective well-being (DeNeve & Cooper, 1998; Hayes & Joseph, 2003; and others). In China extraversion was one of the most important predictors of well-being (Zhang & He, 2010).

Cross-national studies. A 39-nation study of Eysenck's three factors and a 26-nation study of the Big Five found that low neuroticism and high extraversion correlated significantly with national levels of well-being (Steel & Ones, 2002). In the United States and Germany, low neuroticism was the strongest predictor of well-being (Staudinger, Fleeson, & Baltes, 1999). Research in more than 30 countries confirmed that low neuroticism and high extraversion are major correlates (Gomez et al., 2009; Libran & Howard, 2006; Lynn & Steel, 2006).

Apes too. The happiest orangutans in zoos in the United States, Canada and Australia were those rated by keepers as high in extraversion, low in neuroticism and high in agreeableness (Weiss, King, & Perkins, 2006).

Genetic implication. Because neuroticism, extraversion and agreeableness are primarily inherited and influence well-being in so many cultures, the chapter concludes that life satisfaction and happiness have a strong genetic component.

Other traits. A study of US and South Korean students identified four contributors to happiness: autonomy, competence, relatedness and self-esteem (Sheldon, Elliot, Kim, & Kasser, 2001). English university students showed that gratitude is strongly related to well-being: the more grateful people were for their circumstances, the happier they were (Wood, Joseph, & Maltby, 2009).

A downside of conscientiousness. In a German study of nearly 10,000 adults, those highest in conscientiousness who lost their jobs suffered a far greater drop in life satisfaction than those low in conscientiousness (Boyce, Wood, & Brown, 2010).

This section answers the review question on how happy and unhappy people differ in personality: low neuroticism above all, high extraversion, agreeableness and conscientiousness, autonomy, competence, relatedness, self-esteem and gratitude.
sections.simple: Happy people are low in neuroticism and high in extraversion, agreeableness and conscientiousness, a finding confirmed in dozens of countries and even in zoo orangutans. Since these traits are largely inherited, happiness has a strong genetic part. Autonomy, competence, relatedness, self-esteem and gratitude also matter, but highly conscientious people suffer more after losing a job.
keyPoints: Low neuroticism + high extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness = high well-being.
Cross-national (Steel & Ones, 2002; 30+ countries): low neuroticism and high extraversion are major correlates; low neuroticism strongest (US, Germany).
Happiest orangutans: extraverted, low neuroticism, agreeable.
Traits are mainly inherited, so happiness has a strong genetic component.
Autonomy, competence, relatedness, self-esteem, gratitude help; conscientious people hit harder by job loss.

sections.heading: Self-Efficacy and Internal Locus of Control
sections.detailed:
Both Bandura's self-efficacy and Rotter's internal locus of control are positively related to life satisfaction. In general, we are happiest when we feel competent to cope with life and in control of the reinforcers that matter to us.

Studies in Germany and Australia confirmed that feelings of self-mastery and being in control of one's life are strongly related to subjective well-being (Lang & Heckhausen, 2001; Windsor & Anstey, 2010). Autonomy, meaning a strong sense of self-determination, is a significant contributor to happiness (Schmutte & Ryff, 1997; Sheldon et al., 2005).

Trust, emotional stability, self-esteem and the ability to deal positively with stress also correlate with high subjective well-being (DeNeve & Cooper, 1998).

This section ties the chapter together. Rotter's internals were described earlier as happier and higher in subjective well-being; Seligman's learned helplessness is the opposite of perceived control; and here perceived control and competence appear among the core correlates of happiness. The chapter summary lists autonomy, self-esteem, self-efficacy, internal locus of control and a sense of being in control of one's life among the characteristics of the happy personality.
sections.simple: People are happiest when they feel capable (self-efficacy) and in control of what matters (internal locus of control). Self-mastery, autonomy, trust, emotional stability, self-esteem and coping well with stress all go with higher well-being.
keyPoints: Self-efficacy and internal locus of control both relate positively to life satisfaction.
Self-mastery and control strongly linked to well-being (Germany, Australia).
Autonomy (self-determination) contributes significantly to happiness.
Trust, emotional stability, self-esteem and positive coping correlate with well-being.
Connects Rotter's and Seligman's work to happiness.

sections.heading: Thinking Positively
sections.detailed:
Positive emotions such as joy, interest, love and enthusiasm are linked to subjective well-being (Frederickson, 2001), and negative emotions detract from it. This follows from the emotional half of the definition of subjective well-being.

Among eighth- and ninth-graders in Finland, opportunities for self-fulfilment and for social relationships in and out of school correlated highly with subjective well-being (Konu, Lintonen, & Rimpelae, 2002).

Negative emotions show the reverse. Among college students, vengefulness, the desire to seek revenge or hurt others, led to lower life satisfaction (McCullough, Bellah, Kilpatrick, & Johnson, 2001). Research on Holocaust survivors in Israel found that even 60 years after the tragedy, traumatic effects persisted as negative emotions and low subjective well-being (Ben-Zur & Zimmerman, 2005).

Together with the earlier findings on optimism and gratitude, this section supports the conclusion that a positive emotional outlook is among the main features of the happy personality, while lasting negative emotions such as vengefulness or trauma-related distress undermine it.
sections.simple: Positive emotions like joy, interest, love and enthusiasm go with happiness, while negative ones reduce it. Finnish teens with chances for self-fulfilment and friendships were happier, vengeful students were less satisfied, and Holocaust survivors still showed low well-being 60 years later.
keyPoints: Positive emotions (joy, interest, love, enthusiasm) linked to well-being (Frederickson, 2001).
Negative emotions detract from well-being.
Finnish 8th-9th graders: self-fulfilment and social relationships correlate with well-being.
Vengefulness lowers life satisfaction (McCullough et al., 2001).
Holocaust survivors: negative emotions and low well-being 60 years later.

sections.heading: Goals
sections.detailed:
People high and low in subjective well-being differ in their motivations and goals. A research review concluded that life satisfaction is enhanced when people's goals concern personal growth and contributions to the community and are realistic and valued by the culture. People high in life satisfaction were intensely committed to their goals and believed they were making progress toward them (Klug & Maier, 2015; Lyubomirsky, 2001).

Research on more than 3,000 US managers aged 25 to 74 found a strong positive relationship between life satisfaction and a future orientation, including actively planning for the future; the relationship was stronger for older managers (Prenda & Lachman, 2001).

In Germany, the most important life-goal choices relating to happiness involved the characteristics of one's partner, a healthy lifestyle, a proper balance between work and leisure, and social involvement (Headey, Muffels, & Wagner, 2010).

How events are construed. Two large studies, of more than 13,000 college students in 31 countries and more than 7,000 students in 41 countries, found that happy and unhappy people perceive and judge their lives differently. Unhappy people give more weight to what might be wrong in their lives, while happy people look through 'rose-colored glasses' and weigh the positive aspects more heavily (Diener, Lucas, Oishi, & Suh, 2002).

This material, along with geography and Internet use, answers the review question asking how motivations and goals affect subjective well-being.
sections.simple: Happy people pursue realistic goals about personal growth and helping the community, stay committed and feel they're making progress. Planning for the future, a good partner, a healthy lifestyle, work-life balance and social involvement matter, and happy people focus on what's right in their lives rather than what's wrong.
keyPoints: Goals of personal growth and community contribution, realistic and culturally valued, raise life satisfaction.
Commitment and perceived progress toward goals matter (Klug & Maier, 2015; Lyubomirsky, 2001).
3,000+ US managers: future orientation and planning linked to satisfaction, more so for older managers.
Germany: partner characteristics, healthy lifestyle, work-leisure balance, social involvement.
Happy people weigh positives more; unhappy people weigh what is wrong (Diener et al., 2002).

sections.heading: Happiness and Success
sections.detailed:
Which comes first, happiness or success? Are some people happy because they are successful, or successful because they are happy?

Research tends to show that happiness, or subjective well-being, leads to the kinds of behaviour that bring success (Boehm & Lyubomirsky, 2008). People high in subjective well-being are more likely to secure job interviews, to be evaluated more positively by supervisors once employed, and to show superior performance and productivity (Lyubomirsky, King, & Diener, 2005).

This reverses the common assumption that success produces happiness. It parallels the health findings, where happiness was shown to contribute to longevity and health more clearly than health produced happiness. The chapter summary adds that happy people tend to be successful in their careers, to be in better health and to live longer.

For exams, the point to make is the direction of causality: the evidence suggests that happiness comes first and promotes success, not merely the other way round.
sections.simple: Research suggests happiness comes before success, not just after it: happy people get more job interviews, better evaluations from supervisors and are more productive.
keyPoints: Question: does happiness cause success or success cause happiness?
Evidence: happiness leads to behaviours that bring success (Boehm & Lyubomirsky, 2008).
Happy people secure more job interviews, get better supervisor evaluations, perform better (Lyubomirsky et al., 2005).
Happy people tend to be successful, healthier and longer-lived.

sections.heading: Internet Use
sections.detailed:
Does online social media affect happiness? The findings are mixed.

Chinese adolescents showed no significant effect of online social interaction on happiness. Italian college students, however, showed increased subjective well-being and a greater feeling of closeness to their own group and to society after forming social relationships online (Biao-Bin et al., 2006; Contarello & Sarrica, 2007).

Research in Taiwan found a slightly negative effect of Internet use on well-being (Huang, 2010a). A large American study found a stronger negative effect: the more time people spent online, whether browsing, texting, checking news or in chat rooms, the lonelier and less happy they felt (Stepanikova, Nie, & He, 2010). American college students who used personal social media during an assigned classroom task performed worse and had more stress and less happiness than those who did not (Brooks, 2015).

Overall, a large sample from rich and poor nations found that Internet communication made people happier, though some benefited more than others (Penard, Poussing, & Suire, 2013). People with lower incomes or living in developing nations reported greater life satisfaction from the Internet, and more women than men reported feeling empowered by it (Kelly, 2010).

The chapter's conclusion is that the Internet works better for some people than for others in contributing to subjective well-being, which is why the highlights box says happy people spend time on the Internet, or maybe not.
sections.simple: Internet effects on happiness are mixed: no effect for Chinese teens, a boost for Italian students, a small negative effect in Taiwan and a stronger one in the US, where more time online meant more loneliness. Overall the Internet seems to help, especially for low-income people, those in developing nations and women.
keyPoints: China: no effect; Italy: online relationships increased well-being and closeness.
Taiwan: slightly negative; US: more time online = lonelier and less happy (Stepanikova et al., 2010).
Social media during a class task: worse performance, more stress, less happiness (Brooks, 2015).
Overall, Internet communication made people happier (Penard et al., 2013), especially low-income and developing-nation users.
More women than men felt empowered; Internet works better for some than others.

sections.heading: Different Kinds of Happiness: Meaning and Flourishing
sections.detailed:
Three kinds of happiness. As positive psychology developed, Seligman distinguished three types of happiness, or ways of finding satisfaction in life:

1. Positive emotion: the pleasant life, which contains a great deal of positive emotion such as satisfaction, job contentment, serenity and optimism.

2. Engagement: the engaged life, which consists of engagement, involvement, purpose, commitment and absorption in work. For such people time passes quickly, attention is completely focused on the activity, and the sense of self is lost (Seligman, Rashid, & Parks, 2006). Research shows that having a purpose in life is related to finding meaning and also to healthy aging and longevity (Hill & Turiano, 2014). Seligman's own life, built around full engagement in work, fits this type.

3. Meaning: the meaningful life, which involves using one's talents, abilities and strengths to belong to, serve or commit to something larger than the self, such as a religion, organisation, political party or ideal. It produces a sense of satisfaction and the belief that one has lived well. Seligman's research shows that pursuing meaning and engagement correlates much more strongly with happiness than pursuing pleasure (Schueller & Seligman, 2010).

A review question asks which type corresponds most closely to Maslow's self-actualization; the meaningful life, with its use of one's talents and strengths in service of something beyond the self, is the closest match, with the engaged life's absorption also relevant.

Flourishing. In 2012 Seligman published Flourish: A Visionary New Understanding of Happiness and Well-Being. He argued that 'flourishing' describes those at the top of the happiness scale better than happiness or well-being. This group, about 10 to 18 percent of the world's population, not only feel happy but also excel in relationships and accomplishments.

Seligman concluded that happiness alone cannot give life full and deep meaning. To flourish, we must cultivate our talents and abilities, build deep and meaningful relationships, and contribute positively to the world. Happiness, which he now calls positive emotion, is only one of five pillars of the flourishing personality: positive emotion (including happiness and life satisfaction), engagement, relationships, meaning and achievement (Seligman, 2011).

Flourishing differs from his earlier concept of subjective well-being because it goes beyond feeling good and judging life satisfying: it adds relationships and accomplishment, and treats positive emotion as one component rather than the whole goal.
sections.simple: Seligman described three kinds of happiness: the pleasant life (lots of positive emotion), the engaged life (total absorption in work) and the meaningful life (using your strengths to serve something bigger than yourself); meaning and engagement predict happiness more than pleasure. Later he proposed flourishing, achieved by about 10-18 percent of people, built on five pillars: positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning and achievement.
keyPoints: Pleasant life: positive emotion (satisfaction, contentment, serenity, optimism).
Engaged life: involvement and absorption in work; time flies, sense of self lost.
Meaningful life: using strengths to serve something larger than the self; meaning and engagement beat pleasure for happiness.
Flourishing (Flourish, 2012): top 10-18% who are happy and excel in relationships and accomplishments.
Five pillars: positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning, achievement.

sections.heading: Comment
sections.detailed:
Seligman's call for a positive psychology received an enthusiastic response, and the chapter documents its rapid growth.

In 2000, only two years after he introduced the topic, the Journal of Happiness Studies, the first journal in the field, began publication. In 2002 Seligman published the popular book Authentic Happiness: Using the New Positive Psychology to Realize Your Potential for Lasting Fulfillment, which was highly praised. Newsweek described the positive psychology movement as a new age for psychology, and Time magazine put Seligman on its cover with a 40-page special issue.
