At Harvard, the most popular undergraduate course, with more than 800 students, was on positive psychology. In 2006 the Journal of Positive Psychology began publication.

The movement spread beyond academia. In 2012 the Girl Scouts of America created a Science of Happiness Badge, earned through a month-long course in strategies for achieving happiness (Wojcik, 2012). By 2014 more than 10,000 journal articles were being published each year, with seminars, books, magazines and talk shows praising its goals, and by 2015 a Google search for 'happiness' produced almost 350 million hits.

The chapter concludes that positive psychology has become a phenomenally successful and widespread branch of psychology. In an evaluation answer, this popularity can be presented as evidence of impact, alongside the very large empirical literature on subjective well-being reviewed in the chapter.
sections.simple: Positive psychology took off fast: the Journal of Happiness Studies began in 2000, Seligman's Authentic Happiness (2002) was a hit, Time ran a cover story, Harvard's positive psychology course drew 800+ students, and by 2014 over 10,000 articles a year were being published.
keyPoints: Journal of Happiness Studies (2000) - first journal in the field.
Authentic Happiness (2002); Newsweek called it a new age; Time cover and 40-page issue.
Harvard's most popular undergraduate course (800+ students) was positive psychology.
Journal of Positive Psychology (2006); Girl Scouts Science of Happiness Badge (2012).
10,000+ articles per year by 2014; ~350 million Google hits for 'happiness' by 2015.

terms.definition: Study of personality through a single, specific facet (e.g., locus of control, sensation seeking, learned helplessness) researched intensively, rather than a theory of the whole personality.
Rotter's term for people's belief about the source of their reinforcements: their own behaviour (internal) or outside forces (external).
A belief that reinforcement is brought about by our own behaviour and abilities.
A belief that reinforcement is under the control of other people, fate or luck.
Rotter's (1966) self-report inventory of 23 forced-choice item pairs, one internal and one external statement in each, measuring locus of control.
A widely used 40-item locus-of-control test for children, translated into about two dozen languages, with adult and preschool cartoon versions.
The belief that one's own efforts will lead to doing well in school; internals persist more in online courses and resist Internet addiction.
A shared locus of control characterising groups that work or study together, parallel to collective self-efficacy.
Belief that one's own behaviour controls one's health; low in many older, less educated and immigrant Swedes.
The need for varied, novel and complex sensations and experiences, with a willingness to take physical, social, legal and financial risks for them (Zuckerman).
Zuckerman's 40-item forced-choice paper-and-pencil questionnaire measuring sensation seeking; now in its fifth version, with a children's form.
Sensation-seeking component: desire for physical activities involving speed, danger, novelty and defiance of gravity (parachuting, scuba diving, bungee jumping).
Sensation-seeking component: search for novel experiences through travel, music, art or a nonconformist lifestyle.
Sensation-seeking component: need for release in uninhibited social activities such as risky sex, impulsiveness, aggressiveness and antisocial behaviour.
Sensation-seeking component: aversion to repetition, routine work and predictable people, with restless discontent when exposed to them.
Zuckerman's 'good' type, involving the thrill and adventure seeking component.
Zuckerman's 'bad' type: high disinhibition, experience seeking and boredom susceptibility plus high Eysenck psychoticism.
German-developed sensation-seeking test (Roth & Hammelstein, 2012) in German and English; possibly more reliable and valid than the SSS.
Chinese sensation-seeking measure that reliably predicts reckless motorcycling, alcohol and cigarette use and risky sex.

terms.term: Antisocial, adventurous and pro-social risk takers
terms.definition: Levenson's three types of risk takers; antisocial (addicts, criminals) and adventurous (climbers, skydivers) score higher on the SSS than pro-social (police, firefighters).
Zuckerman's description of high sensation seekers: concerned with others only as an audience or source of stimulation, not in a dependent or nurturing way.
Freud's term, applied to high sensation seekers whose images, dreams and daydreams are so vivid that the line between inner stimuli and reality blurs.
A personality style with rigid opinions and prejudiced attitudes; high in low sensation seekers.
Ability to treat ambiguous ideas and situations as challenges rather than threats; low in low sensation seekers, high in high sensation seekers.
A condition resulting from the perception that we have no control over our environment and nothing we do can change our situation.
Two-compartment box divided by a low barrier; animals escape floor shock by jumping into the other compartment.
Immune-system cells that resist viruses, bacteria and tumour cells; weakened in helpless rats and more numerous in optimists.
A way of explaining to ourselves our relative lack of control over the environment; an optimistic style can prevent learned helplessness, a pessimistic style spreads it to all facets of life.
Optimists expect good things to happen to them; pessimists expect bad things to happen to them (Carver & Scheier).
Account in which failure is attributed to a cause: pessimists choose internal, stable, global causes; optimists external, unstable, specific causes.
The pessimist's explanations of bad events ('It's all my fault', 'always this way', 'affects everything'), turning brief local helplessness into lasting general helplessness.
Belief that good things are much more likely to happen to oneself than to others; more common in individualistic cultures and in men.
Telling oneself one will never cope with adversity (showing low self-efficacy), which leads to lack of effort and success.
Seligman's description of depression, whose major symptom is the feeling of being unable to control life events.
A neurotransmitter; its depletion occurs in both learned helplessness and severe depression.
Training (by video in the dental study) that increased patients' sense of control and reduced pain during treatment.
Seligman's movement (late 1990s) holding that psychology should study the best of human functioning: happiness, excellence and optimal growth.
The happy personality: a cognitive evaluation of the quality of one's life plus the possession of positive moods and emotions.
Belief associated with greater happiness among elderly people in Slovakia.
Seligman's first kind of happiness: a great deal of positive emotion such as satisfaction, contentment, serenity and optimism.
Seligman's second kind of happiness: involvement, purpose, commitment and absorption in work, in which time passes quickly and the self is lost.
Seligman's third kind of happiness: using one's talents and strengths to belong to or serve something larger than the self.
Seligman's term for those at the top of the happiness scale (about 10-18% of people) who feel happy and also excel in relationships and accomplishments.
Positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning and achievement (Seligman, 2011).

people.name: Julian Rotter
people.contribution: Social-learning theorist (1916-2014) who proposed locus of control and the I-E Scale; worked at Ohio State and the University of Connecticut.

people.name: Alfred Adler
people.contribution: Rotter met him at Brooklyn College and switched his major to psychology; Rotter likened his brothers to Adler's birth-order descriptions.

people.name: George Kelly
people.contribution: Directed Ohio State's clinical psychology programme while Rotter taught there; both refined their major theories in those 'glory days'.

people.name: Nowicki & Strickland
people.contribution: Developed the 40-item Children's Nowicki-Strickland Internal-External Scale (1973).

people.name: Albert Bandura
people.contribution: Insisted that self-efficacy (belief one can perform an action) overlaps little with locus of control (belief that actions affect outcomes).

people.name: Judge, Erez, Bono & Thoresen
people.contribution: Found a strong relationship between locus of control and self-efficacy in students and sales representatives (2002).

people.name: Marvin Zuckerman
people.contribution: University of Delaware psychologist (1928-) who defined and measured sensation seeking (SSS), identified its four components and good/bad types, and stressed its heritability.

people.name: Hans Eysenck
people.contribution: Noted the hereditary component of sensation seeking and estimated it at 58 percent genetic; his extraversion and psychoticism correlate with sensation seeking.

people.name: Sybil Eysenck
people.contribution: Conducted a twin study with Zuckerman showing an even greater genetic component to sensation seeking.

people.name: Levenson
people.contribution: Identified antisocial, adventurous and pro-social risk takers (1990).

people.name: Raine, Reynolds, Venables & Mednick
people.contribution: Mauritius study: high sensation seekers at 3 scored 12 IQ points higher at 11 (2002).

people.name: Sigmund Freud
people.contribution: His concept of primary-process thought is applied to high sensation seekers' vivid fantasy lives.

people.name: Carl Jung
people.contribution: Jungian extraversion, measured by the MBTI, correlates positively with sensation seeking.

people.name: Martin E. P. Seligman
people.contribution: University of Pennsylvania psychologist (1942-) who discovered learned helplessness, developed explanatory style, founded positive psychology, and proposed three kinds of happiness and flourishing.

people.name: Overmier & Maier
people.contribution: Co-authored Seligman's 1967 dog experiments on inescapable shock and helplessness.

people.name: Hiroto
people.contribution: Demonstrated learned helplessness in humans with inescapable noise (1974).

people.name: Visintainer & Volpicelli
people.contribution: Co-authored the rat tumour-rejection study (1982) showing 70/50/27 percent rejection rates.

people.name: Carver & Scheier
people.contribution: Defined optimists as expecting good things and pessimists bad things; found optimists build better social networks.

people.name: Peterson
people.contribution: Collaborated with Seligman on optimism and health; 'pessimistic parents also have pessimistic children'.

people.name: Ed Diener
people.contribution: Leading subjective well-being researcher: income and satisfaction across 123 nations, happiness and longevity, marriage, culture and rose-coloured perception studies.

people.name: Lyubomirsky
people.contribution: Showed that happiness leads to success and that committed goal pursuit enhances life satisfaction.

studies.title: Lee & Seligman (1997): culture
studies.finding: Americans were more optimistic than Chinese Americans, who were more optimistic than mainland Chinese.

studies.title: Chang, Asakawa & Sanna (2001): Japan
studies.finding: Japanese students were more pessimistic; Americans expected positive events for themselves, Japanese for others.

studies.title: Robinson-Whelen et al. (1997): Alzheimer's caregivers
studies.finding: Caregivers became more pessimistic over four years with more anxiety, stress and health complaints.

studies.title: Brissette, Scheier & Carver (2002): first semester
studies.finding: Optimistic students had less stress and depression during their first semester.

studies.title: Ey et al. (2005): children
studies.finding: Optimistic third- to sixth-graders had fewer depressive symptoms and behaviour problems.

studies.title: El-Anzi (2005); Gibbons et al. (2000): grades
studies.finding: Optimists earned better grades; pessimists were more depressed by low grades.

studies.title: Martin-Krumm et al. (2003): basketball
studies.finding: After supposed failure, optimistic teens were less anxious, more confident and dribbled better.

studies.title: Segerstrom (2001): attention
studies.finding: Pessimists attended to negative stimuli; optimists to both positive and negative.

studies.title: Weber, Vollmann & Renner (2007): flexibility
studies.finding: German optimists were cognitively flexible; pessimists rigid and quick to give up.

studies.title: Sweeny & Shepperd (2010): exam disappointment
studies.finding: Highly optimistic students felt more disappointment after receiving exam scores.

studies.title: Gibson & Sanbonmatsu (2004): gambling
studies.finding: Optimists kept gambling despite consistent losses; pessimists stopped.

studies.title: Lin & Raghubir (2005): unrealistic optimism
studies.finding: More common in individualistic cultures and men.

studies.title: Herbert & Cohen (1993); Weisse (1992): depression and immunity
studies.finding: Over 40 studies: depression suppresses NK activity and alters white blood cell count.

studies.title: Seligman's undergraduate grade study (Zullow & Seligman, 1985; Nolen-Hoeksema et al., 1987)
studies.finding: After 'failure' grades, 70% of pessimists vs 30% of optimists became depressed; explanatory style also predicted depression in third-graders.

studies.title: Chang et al. (2013); Kronstrom et al. (2014): suicide
studies.finding: Pessimists were more likely to take antidepressants and be at risk for suicide.

studies.title: Daraei & Ghaderi (2012): India
studies.finding: More parental formal education predicted more optimistic children.

studies.title: Lau, Rijsdijk & Eley (2006); Mavioglu et al. (2015)
studies.finding: Adolescents' attributional style is influenced by both learning and genes.

studies.title: Orejudo et al. (2012); Ciarrochi & Heaven (2008)
studies.finding: Peer conflict, being treated as less able and low family support lead to helplessness and pessimism.

studies.title: Diener, Ng, Harter & Arora (2010): 123 nations
studies.finding: Higher income means more life satisfaction but not necessarily more happiness.

studies.title: Lottery studies
studies.finding: Large lottery wins usually give only a temporary rise in well-being.

studies.title: Van Boven (2005): materialism
studies.finding: More endorsement of materialistic goals means less happiness and satisfaction.

studies.title: Kahneman et al. (2006): high income
studies.finding: High earners have more stress and less leisure time.

studies.title: Attractiveness studies (US, Canada, England, Germany)
studies.finding: Attractive people are happier, possibly via marriage, jobs and income; stronger in cities; obese Finns less happy.

studies.title: Diener & Chan (2011): 160+ studies
studies.finding: High subjective well-being contributes to longevity and better health.

studies.title: Dolan, Kavetsos & Vlaev (2014): 25 countries
studies.finding: Exercisers report higher life satisfaction.

studies.title: Stone et al. (2010): 300,000 Americans
studies.finding: Well-being high at 18, lowest around 50, higher at 85 than 18.

studies.title: Steptoe, Deaton & Stone (2015): Gallup
studies.finding: Western Europe: dip at 45-54; Eastern Europe, former USSR, Latin America: decline with age.

studies.title: Rayle (2005); Gilman & Huebner (2006): adolescents
studies.finding: Happy teens have parents who value them (stronger for girls), good peers, low anxiety and a sense of control.

studies.title: Guo-Xing & Hai (2006); Ronen et al. (2014)
studies.finding: Happy Chinese teens have educated, harmonious parents; Israeli teens with social support are happier.

studies.title: Kunzmann et al. (2000); Schneider et al. (2006): older Germans
studies.finding: Health problems lower well-being, but attitude toward infirmity matters more than the impairment.

studies.title: Dzuka & Dalbert (2006): Slovakia
studies.finding: Elderly believers in a just world were happier.

studies.title: Netz et al. (2005); Pinquart & Soerensen (2000)
studies.finding: Aerobic and strength exercise and social networks correlate with happiness in older people.

studies.title: Gerstorf et al. (2008, 2010): terminal decline
studies.finding: Happiness declines rapidly in the last 3-5 years of life.

studies.title: Diener et al. (2000); Carr et al. (2014): marriage
studies.finding: In 40+ countries (~60,000 people) married people are happier than unmarried groups.

studies.title: Munsey (2010); Ifcher & Zarghamee (2014): children
studies.finding: Childless people are happier; parents of very young children least happy; unmarried mothers lowest.

studies.title: Hoppmann et al. (2011): 35-year couples
studies.finding: Spouses' happiness rises and falls together.

studies.title: Luhmann & Eid (2009): divorce
studies.finding: Life satisfaction was higher after a second divorce than after the first.

studies.title: Litwin (2005); Jasinskaja-Lahti et al. (2006): immigrants
studies.finding: Social support is crucial for immigrants' well-being in Israel and Finland.

studies.title: Hussain (2014): Denmark
studies.finding: Denmark consistently ranks highest in happiness surveys.

studies.title: Gencoz & Ozlale (2004): Turkey
studies.finding: Giving, not receiving, social support related to well-being.

studies.title: Rice & Steele (2004): ancestry
studies.finding: Americans reflect the well-being level of their ancestral culture.

studies.title: Plaut, Markus & Lachman (2002): US regions
studies.finding: Criteria for happiness differ by region (autonomy, growth, social responsibility).

studies.title: Rentfrow, Mellander & Florida (2009): US states
studies.finding: Well-being highest in west coast/mountain states, lowest in Midwest and South; linked to income, education, tolerance.

studies.title: Le, Lai & Wallen (2009); Postmes & Branscombe (2002): ethnic identity
studies.finding: Stronger ethnic identity and acceptance linked to higher well-being.

studies.title: Broman (1997); Utsey et al. (2002); Prelow et al. (2006): discrimination
studies.finding: Discrimination lowers African Americans' life satisfaction and raises depression.

studies.title: Steel & Ones (2002): 39 and 26 nations
studies.finding: Low neuroticism and high extraversion correlate with national well-being.

studies.title: Staudinger, Fleeson & Baltes (1999)
studies.finding: Low neuroticism was the strongest predictor of well-being in the US and Germany.

studies.title: Weiss, King & Perkins (2006): orangutans
studies.finding: Happiest zoo orangutans were extraverted, low in neuroticism and agreeable.

studies.title: Sheldon et al. (2001): US and South Korea
studies.finding: Autonomy, competence, relatedness and self-esteem contribute to happiness.

studies.title: Wood, Joseph & Maltby (2009): gratitude
studies.finding: More grateful English students were happier.

studies.title: Boyce, Wood & Brown (2010): conscientiousness
studies.finding: Highly conscientious Germans who lost jobs suffered a larger drop in life satisfaction.

studies.title: Lang & Heckhausen (2001); Windsor & Anstey (2010)
studies.finding: Self-mastery and control strongly related to well-being in Germany and Australia.

studies.title: McCullough et al. (2001): vengefulness
studies.finding: Vengefulness led to lower life satisfaction.

studies.title: Ben-Zur & Zimmerman (2005): Holocaust survivors
studies.finding: Negative emotions and low well-being persisted 60 years later.

studies.title: Prenda & Lachman (2001): managers
studies.finding: Future orientation linked to life satisfaction, more for older managers.

studies.title: Headey, Muffels & Wagner (2010): life goals
studies.finding: Partner, healthy lifestyle, work-leisure balance and social involvement are key goals for happiness.

studies.title: Diener, Lucas, Oishi & Suh (2002): 31 and 41 countries
studies.finding: Unhappy people weigh what is wrong; happy people weigh positives.

studies.title: Lyubomirsky, King & Diener (2005): success
studies.finding: Happy people get more interviews, better evaluations and are more productive.

studies.title: Stepanikova, Nie & He (2010): Internet
studies.finding: More time online meant lonelier and less happy Americans.

studies.title: Brooks (2015): social media in class
studies.finding: Social media use during a task meant worse performance, more stress, less happiness.

studies.title: Penard, Poussing & Suire (2013); Kelly (2010)
studies.finding: Internet communication made people happier overall, especially low-income and developing-nation users; women felt empowered.

studies.title: Hill & Turiano (2014): purpose
studies.finding: Purpose in life relates to meaning, healthy aging and longevity.

studies.title: Schueller & Seligman (2010): pursuits
studies.finding: Pursuit of meaning and engagement correlates more with happiness than pursuit of pleasure.

examples.title: Locus of control: two students and a failed test
examples.text: Riya and Arjun both fail a mid-semester test. Riya thinks, 'I didn't practise enough numericals, next time I'll do past papers' (internal). Arjun thinks, 'The paper setter was unfair and it's all luck anyway' (external). Rotter would predict that Riya studies harder next time while Arjun sees little point in trying.

examples.title: Good vs bad sensation seeking on a weekend
examples.text: One friend channels the need for thrills into trekking and river rafting with a certified group (socialized thrill and adventure seeking). Another gets the same buzz from drunk bike racing on highways and picking fights (impulsive, disinhibited, unsocialized). Same underlying need, very different expression.

examples.title: Learned helplessness in a classroom
examples.text: A child who is repeatedly told 'you're just bad at maths' and whose efforts never seem to change the teacher's opinion may stop attempting sums altogether, even when given an easy worksheet, much like Seligman's dogs that stopped jumping the barrier.

examples.title: Optimistic vs pessimistic explanations of rejection
examples.text: After a job rejection, a pessimist says, 'I'm not good enough, I'll never get hired, I fail at everything' (internal, stable, global). An optimist says, 'This company wanted someone with more experience in this exact tool; other openings will be different' (external, unstable, specific).

examples.title: The three kinds of happiness
examples.text: Pleasant life: enjoying a great meal with friends. Engaged life: coding for hours on a project and losing track of time. Meaningful life: volunteering to teach underprivileged children because you believe in education for all.

examples.title: Flourishing beyond feeling good
examples.text: Someone can feel cheerful most days yet have shallow relationships and no achievements they value. Seligman's flourishing would also require deep relationships, engagement, meaning and accomplishment, not just positive feelings.

checks.q: Which pairing of subtitle phrase and facet is correct?
checks.explain: The chapter's subtitle maps taking control to Rotter's locus of control, taking chances to Zuckerman's sensation seeking and finding happiness to Seligman's work.

checks.q: The chapter describes Zuckerman's sensation seeking as
options: a global theory of the whole personality
checks.explain: Zuckerman's research is introduced as concerning a limited-domain aspect of personality (p. 378).

checks.q: Which early event did Rotter say made him aware of how situations affect personality?
options: His father losing his business in the 1929 Depression
checks.explain: Rotter said the family's financial collapse in 1929 began his concern with social injustice and showed him the power of situational conditions (p. 372).

checks.q: At Ohio State University, Rotter worked in the clinical programme directed by
checks.explain: The chapter notes that George Kelly was director of the clinical psychology programme at Ohio State (p. 372).

checks.q: A person who believes that grades depend mainly on the teacher's mood and luck has
checks.explain: Externals believe other people, fate or luck control the reinforcements they receive (p. 372).

checks.q: Which characteristic does the chapter attribute to internals?
options: They see little value in effort
They are less susceptible to attempts to influence them
They pay less attention to environmental cues
checks.explain: Internals are described as less open to influence, more alert to environmental cues and lower in anxiety (p. 373).

checks.q: The I-E Scale consists of
checks.explain: Rotter's I-E Scale has 23 forced-choice alternatives from which the subject picks the statement closer to his or her beliefs (p. 373).

checks.q: Which instrument includes a cartoon version for preschool children?
options: The Need Inventory of Sensation Seeking
checks.explain: An adult form and a cartoon version for preschoolers of the Nowicki-Strickland scale are available (p. 373).

checks.q: According to Heckhausen and Schulz, internal locus of control
options: increases with age and peaks in middle age
checks.explain: People become more internally oriented as they grow older, reaching a peak in middle age (p. 374).

checks.q: Which gender finding is reported for U.S. adults on overall I-E Scale scores?
options: No significant difference between men and women
Women were more external only after age 60
checks.explain: DeBrabander and Boone (1990) found no significant differences between adult men and women in the United States (p. 374).

checks.q: Uba's (1994) comparison showed that the most external group was
checks.explain: Hong Kong Chinese were more external than Chinese Americans, who were more external than European Americans (p. 374).

checks.q: How does the chapter explain the more external orientation of Asians compared with Americans?
options: Asians score higher on sensation seeking
Asian schools use the I-E Scale differently
Asian cultures emphasise collectivism and interdependence, so success is seen as externally caused
checks.explain: The chapter links the difference to collectivism, community reliance and interdependence in Asian culture (p. 374).

checks.q: Research in Turkey found that college students high in internal academic locus of control were
options: far less likely to become addicted to Internet use
more likely to drop out of online courses
more likely to cheat on tests
checks.explain: Iskender and Akin (2010) found internals in academic control were far less likely to become Internet-addicted (p. 375).

checks.q: The idea of a collective locus of control was supported by research on
options: teenagers in Israel during the Gulf War
checks.explain: Austrian entrepreneurial teams highest in internal control performed most efficiently and effectively (p. 375).

checks.q: Zeidner's (1993) study of Israeli adolescents during the Persian Gulf War found that those higher in perceived control
options: had less anxiety and fewer stress symptoms
checks.explain: Teenagers higher in perceived control experienced significantly less anxiety and fewer stress-related symptoms (p. 376).

checks.q: In the study of German nurses, those reporting more stress and burnout scored
options: higher in internal locus of control
higher in external locus of control
checks.explain: Nurses with more work stress and burnout scored higher in external control (p. 375).

checks.q: Which is reported for internally oriented cardiac patients?
options: They cooperate better with staff and are released earlier
They trust their doctors more and stay longer
They are slower to return to work
checks.explain: Internals with cardiac problems cooperate better with hospital staff, are released earlier and return to work sooner (p. 376).

checks.q: Cancer patients in the Netherlands who were high in external control
options: had more trust in their oncologists
checks.explain: Hillen et al. (2014) found externals had more trust in their oncologists (p. 376).

checks.q: Which parental behaviour is associated with an internal locus of control in children?
options: Consistent discipline and praise for achievement
checks.explain: Parents of internals were supportive, praised achievements, were consistent in discipline and not authoritarian (p. 377).

checks.q: External control beliefs in children tend to increase with
options: the presence of an adult male role model
checks.explain: External beliefs are likely in homes without an adult male role model and tend to increase with number of siblings (p. 376).

checks.q: A major difference between locus of control and self-efficacy is that
options: locus of control is generalised, while self-efficacy is situation-specific
self-efficacy is generalised, while locus of control is situation-specific
only locus of control involves perceived control
self-efficacy is inherited, locus of control is learned
checks.explain: The chapter states locus of control generalises over many situations whereas self-efficacy tends to be specific to a situation (p. 377).

checks.q: Bandura's position on self-efficacy and locus of control was that
options: there is little overlap between them
self-efficacy is a type of external control
locus of control should replace self-efficacy
checks.explain: Bandura insisted the concepts overlap little: belief in producing actions differs from belief that actions affect outcomes (p. 377).

checks.q: Zuckerman's definition of sensation seeking includes a willingness to take which kinds of risk?
checks.explain: Zuckerman's definition names physical, social, legal and financial risks (p. 378).

checks.q: According to the chapter, the hereditary component of sensation seeking was first noted by
checks.explain: The chapter says the trait has a large hereditary component initially noted by Eysenck (p. 378).

checks.q: How did Zuckerman establish the validity of the SSS?
options: By comparing scores of people who sought novel, risky activities with those who avoided them
By correlating it with the I-E Scale
By measuring heart rate during parachute jumps only
checks.explain: Those who deliberately sought unusual activities scored high and those preferring less venturesome activities scored low (p. 378).

checks.q: Which scale has been shown to be reliable and valid in China for predicting reckless motorcycle riding?
checks.explain: The Brief Sensation Seeking Scale predicts reckless motorcycle riding, alcohol and cigarette use and risky sex in China (p. 379).

checks.q: An aversion to routine work and predictable people describes which component?
checks.explain: Boredom susceptibility is an aversion to repetitive experiences, routine work and predictable people (p. 379).

checks.q: Zuckerman's 'bad' sensation seeking is characterised by
options: high thrill and adventure seeking only
low scores on all four components
high disinhibition, experience seeking, boredom susceptibility and psychoticism
checks.explain: Impulsive unsocialized sensation seeking involves high disinhibition, experience seeking and boredom susceptibility plus high psychoticism (p. 379).

checks.q: According to Zuckerman's own account, which component does NOT decline with age?
checks.explain: Zuckerman wrote that thrill and adventure seeking and disinhibition fall rapidly with age but experience seeking does not change (p. 380).

checks.q: On which component do women score higher than men?
checks.explain: Men scored higher on three components; women scored higher on experience seeking (p. 380).

checks.q: In Levenson's (1990) research, which group had the LOWEST sensation-seeking scores?
options: Antisocial risk takers such as criminals
Adventurous risk takers such as mountain climbers
Pro-social risk takers such as police officers and firefighters
checks.explain: Antisocial and adventurous risk takers scored significantly higher than pro-social risk takers, whose motives involve other factors (p. 381).

checks.q: In Zuckerman's research, the percentage of high versus low sensation seekers reporting risky homosexual encounters was
checks.explain: Zuckerman found 16 percent of high and 7 percent of low sensation seekers reported risky homosexual encounters (p. 381).

checks.q: Rosenbloom's research in Israel found that high sensation seekers prefer
options: hot colours such as red and orange
checks.explain: High sensation seekers prefer hot colours such as red and orange rather than pastels (p. 382).

checks.q: Why did researchers think high sensation seekers performed poorly in low-level jobs?
options: The jobs were not stimulating enough for them
They had an external locus of control
checks.explain: Reio and Sanders-Reio suggested lower-level jobs might not be sufficiently stimulating for high sensation seekers (p. 382).

checks.q: Zuckerman described high sensation seekers as 'egocentrically extraverted', meaning they
options: relate to others in a dependent, nurturing way
are concerned with others mainly as an audience or source of stimulation
checks.explain: Egocentric extraversion means others matter mainly as an audience or source of stimulation, not in a dependent or nurturing way (p. 382).

checks.q: What relationship was found between sensation seeking and neuroticism?
checks.explain: Investigations of sensation seeking and neuroticism showed no correlation (p. 382).

checks.q: In the Mauritius study, children high in sensation seeking at age 3
options: scored 12 points higher on intelligence tests at age 11
earned much better school grades at age 11
showed no difference from low scorers
checks.explain: High sensation seekers at age 3 scored 12 points higher on intelligence tests at 11 (Raine et al., 2002, p. 383).

checks.q: Zuckerman explained the vivid fantasy life of high sensation seekers by suggesting that
options: when they cannot find novelty externally they look inward
checks.explain: If high sensation seekers cannot find novel experiences in external situations, they may create a fantasy world (p. 383).

checks.q: Men high in sensation seeking showed LOW interest in which occupation?
checks.explain: High-SSS men's scores correlated negatively with business jobs such as accountant, purchasing agent and banker (p. 383).

checks.q: Women with high SSS scores showed high interest in which profession?
checks.explain: High-SSS women scored high for lawyer and low for elementary school teacher (p. 383).

checks.q: Low sensation seekers tend to score high on
checks.explain: Low sensation seekers scored high on authoritarianism, typified by rigid opinions and prejudice (p. 383).

checks.q: Low sensation seekers view ambiguous ideas and situations as
checks.explain: Low sensation seekers have low tolerance for ambiguity and see it as threatening (p. 383).

checks.q: Eysenck estimated that what percentage of sensation seeking is genetic?
checks.explain: A study by Eysenck suggested 58 percent of the trait was accounted for by genetic factors (p. 384).

checks.q: Zuckerman explained the higher sensation seeking of first-borns and only children by
options: the greater stimulation and attention they receive from parents early in life
checks.explain: First-borns and only-borns receive more early stimulation and attention, predisposing them to sensation seeking (p. 384).

checks.q: Why does Zuckerman's work fall into a different category from social-learning approaches?
options: Because he emphasises the heritability of sensation seeking
checks.explain: His emphasis on heritability places his work apart from approaches focusing on situations and learning (p. 385).

checks.q: Which adjective did LOW sensation seekers choose to describe themselves?
checks.explain: Table 14.3 lists frightened, panicky, tense, nervous, shaky, fearful, worried and upset for low sensation seekers (p. 385).

checks.q: In the first part of the dog experiment Seligman witnessed, the dogs were
options: trained to jump a barrier for food
allowed to escape shock by pressing a panel
classically conditioned to associate a tone with shock
exposed to novel stimuli to measure sensation seeking
checks.explain: The dogs were conditioned to associate a high-pitched sound with an electric shock in a Pavlovian procedure (p. 385).

checks.q: Learned helplessness is defined in the chapter as a condition resulting from
options: too much control over the environment
a need for novel and complex sensation
a belief that luck controls reinforcement
the perception that we have no control over our environment
checks.explain: The glossary defines learned helplessness as resulting from the perception that we have no control over our environment (p. 385).

checks.q: Seligman explained the dogs' failure to escape by suggesting that they had
options: learned in the first phase that their actions could not change the situation
been physically injured by the shock
not been able to see the barrier
checks.explain: Seligman suggested the dogs learned they were helpless to change their situation and this generalised to the second phase (p. 386).

checks.q: What did the dogs do when shocked in the shuttle box?
options: Lay down, whimpered and made no effort to escape
Pressed a lever to stop the shock
checks.explain: The dogs lay down, whimpered and made no effort to escape (p. 386).

checks.q: In Hiroto's (1974) study, subjects in the experimental group
options: could stop the noise with an easy sequence
could not stop the noise because no correct button sequence existed
checks.explain: Experimental subjects were told a button sequence would stop the noise, but no correct sequence existed (p. 386).

checks.q: A meta-analysis of 132 studies found that the effects of inescapable aversive stimulation were
options: weaker in humans than in animals
even stronger in humans than in animals
checks.explain: The meta-analysis found effects of inescapable shock were even stronger in human than animal subjects (p. 387).

checks.q: Prisoners subjected to inescapable aversive conditions showed which symptoms?
options: They became compliant and stopped trying to change their conditions
They became more aggressive and resistant
They developed an internal locus of control
checks.explain: The prisoners showed the same symptoms as lab subjects: compliance and no attempt to change conditions (p. 387).

checks.q: Seligman's reaction to learning that his findings were used in interrogation was that he was
checks.explain: Seligman said he was 'grieved and horrified' at the use of his experiments (p. 387).

checks.q: In Thompson et al.'s (1993) study of cancer patients, better psychological adjustment was associated with
options: better physical condition regardless of perceived control
higher perceived control, even among severely debilitated patients
checks.explain: Patients who believed they could influence illness, recovery and emotions adjusted better than healthier patients low in perceived control (p. 387).

checks.q: Which dental patients benefited most from the stress inoculation training video?
options: Those with no desire for control
Those who watched the local sights video
Those low in control but with a strong desire for control
checks.explain: Patients with low control but a strong desire for greater control benefited most (p. 388).

checks.q: In the Visintainer, Volpicelli and Seligman (1982) study, what percentage of rats given inescapable shock rejected the tumour?
checks.explain: Only 27 percent of the inescapable-shock rats rejected the malignant cells, compared with 50 percent (no shock) and 70 percent (escapable) (p. 388).

checks.q: Maier, Laudenslager and Ryan (1985) found that in rats given inescapable shock
options: T-cells stopped multiplying rapidly and NK cells lost their ability to destroy infections
checks.explain: Learned helplessness weakened the immune system: T-cells did not multiply and NK cells lost their effectiveness (p. 388).

checks.q: According to the attribution model, pessimists attribute failure to causes that are
checks.explain: The summary states pessimists attribute failures to internal, stable and global causes (p. 404).

checks.q: Seligman proposed explanatory style because he believed health is affected not only by lack of control but also by
options: how we explain that lack of control to ourselves
checks.explain: It is not only lack of control but how we explain it to ourselves that matters (p. 388).

checks.q: In the study of nuns, optimism expressed in life stories written in their early 20s predicted
options: a significantly lower death rate 60 years later
higher blood pressure in old age
checks.explain: Nuns showing optimism in early writings had a significantly lower death rate 60 years later (Danner et al., 2001, p. 390).

checks.q: Segerstrom and Taylor (1998) found that optimistic first-semester law students had
checks.explain: Optimistic law students had a significantly greater number of T-cells and NK cells (p. 389).

checks.q: Lee and Seligman (1997) found which order of optimism, from most to least optimistic?
checks.explain: American subjects were more optimistic than Chinese Americans, who were more optimistic than mainland Chinese (p. 390).

checks.q: Adults who were primary caregivers for relatives with Alzheimer's disease
options: grew increasingly pessimistic over four years
checks.explain: Caregivers grew increasingly pessimistic over a four-year period and had more anxiety, stress and health complaints (pp. 390-391).

checks.q: Segerstrom (2001) found that students high in optimism
options: attended to both positive and negative stimuli
checks.explain: Pessimists attended more to negative stimuli; optimists attended to both positive and negative stimuli (p. 391).

checks.q: Among college students gambling at a casino, optimists
options: were more likely to stop after losing
checks.explain: Optimists were far more likely to keep gambling during a losing streak, maintaining positive expectations (p. 392).

checks.q: In Seligman's semester study, what percentage of pessimistic students who received disappointing grades became depressed?
checks.explain: 70 percent of pessimists with disappointing grades became depressed compared with 30 percent of optimists (p. 393).

checks.q: Which symptom appears in BOTH learned helplessness and depression in Table 14.4?
checks.explain: Passivity, norepinephrine depletion and ulcers/stress appear in both columns of Table 14.4 (p. 393).

checks.q: By about what age does a consistent explanatory style develop?
checks.explain: A consistent explanatory style develops by about age 8 and is strongly affected by parents' style (p. 394).

checks.q: Studies in India found children's optimism was strongly influenced by
options: their parents' level of formal education
checks.explain: The greater the parents' formal education, the greater the optimism of their children (Daraei & Ghaderi, 2012, p. 394).

checks.q: Seligman applied his findings outside the laboratory by
options: proposing a programme of exercises to teach optimism
founding the Girl Scouts happiness badge
checks.explain: Seligman proposed a programme of exercises to teach optimism to adults and children (p. 394).

checks.q: The learned helplessness work led Seligman to extend his ideas to
checks.explain: He extended his ideas to positive psychology and factors influencing subjective well-being (pp. 394-395).

checks.q: Seligman advanced positive psychology
options: in the late 1990s during his term as APA president
in the 1960s during his dog experiments
in the 1970s at the University of Delaware
checks.explain: Positive psychology was advanced by Seligman in the late 1990s while he was APA president (p. 395).

checks.q: Seligman believed psychology should deal with
options: the best of human functioning, such as happiness and excellence
checks.explain: He thought psychology should address happiness, excellence and optimal human growth (p. 395).

checks.q: In 2010 Seligman ranked himself in terms of positive feelings and emotions among
checks.explain: Seligman ranked himself among the lowest 30 percent in positive feelings and emotions (p. 395).

checks.q: What happened to Seligman when he was 13?
options: His father suffered a severe stroke that left him almost helpless

practice.q: Explain Rotter's concept of locus of control. How is it assessed, and how do internals and externals differ in behaviour, culture and health?
practice.answer:
Introduction. Julian Rotter, a social-learning theorist, explained behaviour by considering both external reinforcements and internal cognitions. His research showed that people differ in where they believe their reinforcements come from, a generalised belief he called locus of control. It is one of the most studied variables in psychology and a classic example of the limited-domain approach.

Internal versus external. People with an internal locus of control believe the reinforcement they receive depends on their own behaviour and abilities. People with an external locus of control believe it is controlled by other people, fate or luck, and they feel powerless against outside forces. Because externals expect their efforts to make no difference, they see little reason to try; internals feel a firm grip on their lives and act accordingly. Internals perform better at work, resist influence, value their skills, attend to environmental cues, and report lower anxiety, higher self-esteem and greater happiness.

Assessment. Rotter's Internal-External (I-E) Scale (1966) has 23 forced-choice pairs; respondents choose one statement in each pair, one internal and one external (for example, misfortunes due to bad luck versus to people's own mistakes). The 40-item Children's Nowicki-Strickland scale, translated into about two dozen languages, has adult and preschool cartoon versions, and variants measure specific domains such as dieting.

Age and gender. Internality grows with age, peaking in middle age, and cognitive training raised it in adults aged 60-75. Gender findings are mixed: Norwegian girls were more internal than boys, US adults showed no difference, while women in England and China were more external than men.

Culture. Native Africans and American-born Blacks score more external than American-born Whites; higher socioeconomic status predicts internality in Botswana and the US; Moroccan and Turkish immigrants in the Netherlands are more external than natives. Collectivist cultures (China, Lebanon) are more external than individualistic ones (US, South Africa), and acculturation increases internality (Hong Kong Chinese > Chinese Americans > European Americans in externality).

Behaviour and mental health. Internals adapt to change, have stronger mental skills and higher job satisfaction; students with internal academic control persist in online courses and avoid Internet addiction; internal teams perform better. Internals have fewer emotional problems and less alcoholism, cope better with stress (German nurses), adjust better to leaving home, and are less anxious, depressed, lonely or suicidal. Israeli teens high in perceived control suffered less anxiety during the Gulf War. Externals are prone to burnout, hopelessness, psychotic episodes, cyberbullying victimisation and hoarding.

Physical health. Internals have lower blood pressure and fewer heart attacks, cooperate with hospital staff, leave hospital and return to work sooner, recover better after bypass surgery, wear seat belts, exercise, quit smoking and get cancer screening. Some studies, however, found that internals took less general care of their health.

Development and evaluation. Locus of control is learned from parents: supportive, praising, consistent, non-authoritarian parents who encourage independence raise internals, while poverty, many siblings and absence of a male role model foster externality. It correlates strongly with Bandura's self-efficacy, though Bandura argued they differ.

Conclusion. Locus of control is a rigorously researched, objectively measured belief that predicts a remarkable range of outcomes, with internality generally linked to better adjustment, health and achievement.

practice.q: Define sensation seeking. Describe its assessment, four components, Zuckerman's good and bad types, and the research on characteristics and behaviour of high sensation seekers.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Marvin Zuckerman of the University of Delaware has studied sensation seeking since the 1970s as a limited-domain aspect of personality. He defines it as a desire for varied, novel, complex and intense sensations and experiences, with a willingness to take physical, social, legal and financial risks to obtain them; in short, 'taking chances'. The trait has a large hereditary component.

Assessment. The Sensation Seeking Scale (SSS) is a 40-item forced-choice questionnaire, now in Form V, with a children's version. Zuckerman validated it by showing that volunteers for novel experiments, people in dangerous jobs and drug or sexual experimenters scored high, while risk-avoiders scored low. Items contrast, for instance, wild parties with quiet conversation, or wanting to try parachuting with never wanting to. Newer instruments include the German Need Inventory of Sensation Seeking, possibly more reliable and valid, and China's Brief Sensation Seeking Scale.

Four components (factor analysis). Thrill and adventure seeking: physical activities involving speed, danger and defiance of gravity. Experience seeking: novelty through travel, music, art or a nonconformist lifestyle. Disinhibition: release through uninhibited social activity, risky sex, impulsiveness and aggression. Boredom susceptibility: aversion to routine and predictable people.

Good and bad sensation seeking. Non-impulsive socialized (good) sensation seeking involves thrill and adventure seeking. Impulsive unsocialized (bad) sensation seeking involves high disinhibition, experience seeking and boredom susceptibility plus high psychoticism.

Characteristics. Differences appear early: second-graders high in the trait chose a shark video over a funny bunny. Sensation seeking rises in middle school and falls in the twenties; thrill seeking and disinhibition decline with age but experience seeking does not, as Zuckerman noted in his own life. Education makes no difference. Men score higher overall and on three components; women score higher on experience seeking. Westerners and Whites score higher than Asians and non-Whites.

Behaviour. High scorers are overrepresented among skydivers, firefighters, riot police and race-car drivers, volunteer for combat units, and travel to hazardous places. Levenson found antisocial and adventurous risk takers scored higher than pro-social ones. High sensation seekers use and sell drugs earlier, drink, shoplift, commit delinquency, drive fast and drunk, have more accidents, gamble online and take sexual risks (16 versus 7 percent risky encounters), making high-sensation-seeking gay men a high-risk group for AIDS. They cross against red lights, prefer hot colours, have more tattoos, cheat more, may misuse computers and perform poorly in dull jobs.

Personality, cognition and interests. They are egocentrically extraverted, linked with psychoticism but not neuroticism, high in openness, conscientiousness, autonomy and assertiveness. Intelligence correlates modestly (Mauritian children scored 12 IQ points higher), but grades are not better; they are original and prone to vivid primary-process fantasy. They prefer science and helping professions over clerical and business work, and hold liberal, atheistic, permissive attitudes, whereas low scorers are authoritarian and intolerant of ambiguity.

Conclusion. Sensation seeking is largely inherited (Eysenck: 58 percent), yet shaped by culture, parents, schools and possibly birth order. It has commonsense appeal and continues to generate research.

practice.q: Describe Seligman's early research on learned helplessness with dogs and humans. How does learned helplessness affect physical health, and how is it related to depression?
practice.answer:
Introduction. Learned helplessness is a condition resulting from the perception that we have no control over our environment. Martin Seligman discovered it by accident in the mid-1960s at the University of Pennsylvania and built a research programme that later led to explanatory style and positive psychology.

The original observation. Dogs were first classically conditioned to associate a tone with unavoidable shock. They were then placed in a shuttle box where jumping a low wall would escape floor shock. Instead of escaping, they lay down and whimpered. Seligman reasoned that they had learned in the first phase that nothing they did mattered, and this expectation generalised to a situation where escape was possible.

Experimental dogs. In controlled experiments (Overmier & Seligman, 1967; Seligman & Maier, 1967), harnessed dogs received inescapable shock and were then tested in the shuttle box against control dogs. Controls ran about, accidentally jumped the barrier and escaped faster on each trial. Experimental dogs ran for about 30 seconds, gave up, lay down whimpering, and never learned to escape, even when lured with food.

Human studies. Hiroto (1974) exposed people to loud noise that a button sequence supposedly stopped, though no sequence worked; controls could stop it. Later, when a simple hand movement would end the noise, experimental subjects sat passively. Helplessness also arises from watching similar helpless models, and a meta-analysis of 132 studies found effects even stronger in humans than animals, across students, children, the elderly, unemployed women and psychiatric patients. Everyday sources include uncontrollable noise and cyberbullying. The techniques were even used in interrogating prisoners, who became compliant; Seligman was horrified.

Physical health. Rats injected with tumour cells rejected them in 70 percent of cases with escapable shock, 50 percent with no shock and only 27 percent with inescapable shock. Rats made helpless when young failed to reject tumours as adults, while early mastery 'immunized'. Helplessness weakened rats' immune systems: T-cells stopped multiplying and NK cells lost their effectiveness. Helplessness was easier to produce in male than female rats. Conversely, perceived control helped cancer patients adjust and stress inoculation increased dental patients' control and reduced pain.

Depression. Seligman found a strong link between helplessness and depression, which he called the 'ultimate pessimism'. Table 14.4 shows shared symptoms: passivity, difficulty learning that responses produce outcomes, norepinephrine depletion, ulcers and stress. Depression also weakens immunity, suppressing NK cells. Explanatory style determines who becomes depressed: a pessimistic style makes helplessness long-lasting and general, because pessimists explain failure in personal, permanent and pervasive (internal, stable, global) terms. In Seligman's semester study, 70 percent of pessimists versus 30 percent of optimists became depressed after a grade they considered failure, and similar results occurred in third-graders. Pessimists are also more likely to use antidepressants and be at suicide risk.

Conclusion. Learned helplessness, supported by hundreds of studies, links uncontrollable experience to passivity, illness and depression, and Seligman applied it through programmes teaching optimism.

practice.q: Distinguish between optimistic and pessimistic explanatory styles. Discuss their effects on health, longevity, performance and cognition, and the downside of optimism.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Seligman extended learned helplessness by arguing that health depends not only on lack of control but on how we explain it. Explanatory style is a way of explaining to ourselves our relative lack of control; an optimistic style prevents helplessness, while a pessimistic style spreads it to all facets of life. Optimists expect good things, pessimists bad things (Carver & Scheier).

The attributional distinction. According to the attribution model, pessimists attribute failure to internal, stable and global causes, making personal, permanent and pervasive explanations ('It's all my fault', 'It will always be this way', 'It affects everything'). Optimists attribute failure to external, unstable and specific causes. Thus a pessimistic style turns brief, local helplessness into lasting, generalised helplessness, and failure becomes depression; in optimists failure brings only brief demoralisation (70 versus 30 percent depressed after disappointing grades).

Health. Pessimists believe actions matter little, so they neglect smoking, diet, exercise and medical care. Optimists get sick less and care for themselves when ill; pessimistic students had twice as many infections. Optimists recover faster from family loss and medical procedures, manage stress better, survive longer after breast cancer recurrence and report better quality of life. They have stronger immune systems (more T-cells and NK cells in law students), recover better from heart attacks and surgery, and have lower blood pressure than pessimists. Optimistic men facing HIV had less distress, without increased risky sex.

Longevity. Nuns whose early writings were optimistic had lower death rates 60 years later; optimistic patients had 19 percent greater longevity over 30 years; elderly English optimists were healthier.

Age, culture and stress. Over-65s are more optimistic. Optimism reduced depression, anxiety and sleep problems in caregiving grandmothers and Kuwaiti and Omani students. Americans are more optimistic than Chinese Americans, who exceed mainland Chinese; Japanese and Kuwaiti students are more pessimistic. Caring for an Alzheimer's relative increased pessimism, while optimism protected students, adults and children from stress and depression.

Performance and cognition. Optimists earn better grades and are less upset by poor ones; French teenage optimists performed better after a supposed dribbling failure. Pessimists focus on negative stimuli while optimists attend to both; optimists are flexible, pessimists rigid and quick to abandon goals.

Downside. Unrealistic optimism can lead to excess drinking and drug use, greater disappointment over exam scores and continued gambling despite losses. It is more common in individualistic cultures and in men. Unrealistic pessimism, with low self-efficacy, reduces effort and success.

Development. A consistent style forms by about age 8, mirrors parents' style, and is shaped by parental education, genes, bullying, harsh schools, poverty and low family support.

Conclusion. Explanatory style is a powerful predictor of health, longevity, achievement and depression; realistic optimism is most adaptive, and Seligman showed it can be taught.

practice.q: What does positive psychology research reveal about the factors associated with subjective well-being?
practice.answer:
Introduction. Seligman launched positive psychology in the late 1990s as APA president, arguing that psychology should study the best of human functioning. The happy personality is studied as subjective well-being or life satisfaction: a cognitive evaluation of the quality of one's life together with positive moods and emotions.

Money. Money does not buy happiness, but lack of money causes unhappiness; adequate income is necessary but not sufficient. Across 123 nations higher earners were more satisfied but not necessarily happier. Lottery wins give temporary boosts, materialism lowers happiness, and high earners have more stress and less leisure.

Attractiveness and health. Attractive people are happier, probably through better marriage, job and income prospects, especially in cities; obese-appearing Finns are less happy. Health is necessary but not sufficient, while happiness promotes health and longevity (160+ studies); exercisers are more satisfied.

Age. Among 300,000 Americans, well-being was high at 18, dipped around 50 and rose by 85, though other countries differ. Happy adolescents have caring, educated, harmonious parents, good peers, social support and a sense of control. In old age, attitude toward infirmity, belief in a just world, exercise and social networks matter, with a decline in the final three to five years.

Marriage and support. Married people are happier in 40+ countries, but children reduce happiness and unmarried mothers are least happy. Spouses' happiness moves together. Social support predicts well-being, especially for immigrants.

Culture and geography. Denmark ranks happiest; wealthy and individualistic nations are happier. In China and Turkey social support matters little, and in Turkey giving support counts more than receiving it. Descendants of immigrants reflect their ancestral culture's well-being. US regions define happiness differently, and well-being is highest in west coast and mountain states, linked to income, education and tolerance.

Race and ethnicity. Strong ethnic identity raises well-being; discrimination lowers life satisfaction and increases depression among African Americans.

Personality and control. Low neuroticism and high extraversion, agreeableness and conscientiousness predict well-being across dozens of countries, even in orangutans, implying a genetic component. Autonomy, competence, relatedness, self-esteem and gratitude help, though conscientious people suffer more after job loss. Self-efficacy, internal locus of control, self-mastery, trust and emotional stability correlate with happiness.

Positive thinking and goals. Positive emotions raise and negative emotions such as vengefulness or trauma lower well-being. Committed pursuit of realistic growth and community goals, future planning, work-leisure balance and social involvement increase satisfaction, and happy people weigh the positives in their lives.

Success and Internet. Happiness leads to success: happy people get interviews, positive evaluations and higher productivity. Internet effects are mixed, helping low-income and developing-nation users and women more.

Conclusion. Many circumstances are necessary but not sufficient; personality, control and outlook are strong predictors. Seligman later distinguished pleasant, engaged and meaningful lives and proposed flourishing, built on positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning and achievement.

practice.q: How do the global and the limited-domain approaches to personality differ? Use this chapter to illustrate the limited-domain approach.
practice.answer:
Global theories, such as those of Freud or Jung covered earlier in the book, try to explain the whole personality within one comprehensive system. The limited-domain approach instead takes one specific facet of personality, defines it narrowly, measures it objectively and relates it to many behaviours through research.

This chapter illustrates the approach with three facets. Rotter's locus of control ('taking control') is measured by the I-E Scale and related to age, culture, work behaviour, mental and physical health and parenting. Zuckerman's sensation seeking ('taking chances'), which the chapter calls a limited-domain aspect of personality, is measured by the Sensation Seeking Scale and related to risk taking, drug use, personality, cognition and job interests. Seligman's learned helplessness, called a limited-domain facet, grew into research on explanatory style and happiness.

Each programme rests on a large, cross-cultural empirical base rather than clinical speculation, and each links to other concepts (self-efficacy, extraversion, the five-factor model). The cost is breadth: none offers a full account of the whole person. (Note: the chapter itself mostly shows the approach in use; the formal global versus limited-domain contrast is drawn in the part introduction.)

practice.q: If external locus-of-control people learned that a tornado was approaching, would they be likely to act to protect themselves? Explain.
practice.answer:
Externals would be less likely to take protective action. Rotter defined an external locus of control as the belief that reinforcements are controlled by other people, fate or luck, so externals feel powerless against outside forces. Because they believe their own behaviour makes little difference to outcomes, they see little value in exerting effort to improve their situation; why try when you expect not to control present or future events? Faced with a tornado, an external might feel that whatever happens is a matter of fate.

Internals, by contrast, believe outcomes depend on their own behaviour and abilities. They are described as having a firm grip on their lives, being alert to environmental cues that guide behaviour, and placing high value on their skills, so they would be more likely to seek shelter and protect family and property.

The research supports this reasoning. Internals are more health-conscious (wearing seat belts, getting screened for cancer), cope better with stress, and Israeli adolescents higher in perceived control experienced less anxiety and fewer stress symptoms during Scud missile attacks in the 1990 Gulf War. Externals are more prone to hopelessness and indecision in new situations.

practice.q: What parental behaviours foster an internal locus of control in children?
practice.answer:
Locus of control is learned in childhood and is directly related to parental behaviour. Parents of children with an internal locus of control were found to be:

1. Highly supportive of their children.
2. Generous with praise for achievement, which is positive reinforcement that teaches children their actions produce rewards.
3. Consistent in discipline, so consequences reliably follow behaviour.
4. Not authoritarian.
5. Encouraging of independence as their children grow older, giving them direct experience of control.

By contrast, external beliefs are more common in homes without an adult male role model, and they increase with the number of siblings. Children in large single-parent families headed by women, children of depressed mothers with little education or income, and children from low-income families tend to develop an external orientation or a lower sense of control.

In social-learning terms, consistent and contingent reinforcement in a supportive home teaches the child that behaviour and outcomes are connected, whereas unpredictable, resource-poor environments teach that outcomes are outside one's control. Internals also tend to have parents who are themselves high in internal control.

practice.q: How do the concepts of locus of control and self-efficacy differ? In what ways are they similar?
practice.answer:
Similarities. Judge, Erez, Bono and Thoresen (2002), studying college students and sales representatives, found a strong relationship between Rotter's locus of control and Bandura's self-efficacy. Some researchers argue that both deal with our perception or belief about how much control we have over events in our lives and about our ability to cope with them. Both are also positively related to life satisfaction: people are happiest when they feel competent and in control of important reinforcers. The chapter even suggests a collective locus of control parallel to collective self-efficacy.

Differences. Locus of control is a generalised belief that applies across many situations, whereas self-efficacy tends to be specific to a particular situation. Bandura insisted the overlap is small: a belief that one can carry out certain actions (self-efficacy) is not the same as a belief that actions affect outcomes (locus of control). Locus of control asks whether behaviour produces reinforcement; self-efficacy asks whether I can perform the behaviour.

Thus a person could believe effort generally pays off (internal) yet doubt their ability in a specific task (low self-efficacy). The chapter also links low self-efficacy to unrealistic pessimism, which reduces effort.

practice.q: Discuss the relative importance of heredity and environment in determining sensation seeking.
practice.answer:
Heredity. Research consistently shows a strong hereditary basis for sensation seeking. Eysenck estimated that 58 percent of the trait is genetic, and a twin study by Zuckerman and Sybil Eysenck found an even greater genetic component. The chapter summary calls the trait primarily inherited, and this emphasis places Zuckerman apart from behavioural and social-learning approaches.

Environment. Learning still matters. Small but significant differences between 14- to 20-year-olds in Turkey and Wales in motivation for risky behaviour suggest cultural learning. Parents influence the trait: low-sensation-seeking parents may be fearful, protective and forbidding, while high-sensation-seeking parents reinforce unusual activities. Swedish teens high in sensation seeking and impulsivity committed fewer crimes if they attended privileged schools, and institutionally raised high sensation seekers got into less trouble than those raised in private homes, showing that environment shapes how the trait is expressed. Early studies found first-borns and only children higher in sensation seeking, explained by greater early stimulation, though later English research found no birth-order effect.

Conclusion. Heredity sets the level of sensation seeking to a large extent, while culture, parenting, schooling and possibly birth order modify its level and channel its expression.

practice.q: Describe the occupational interests and political and religious attitudes of high sensation seekers.
practice.answer:
Occupational interests. Because they need varied, stimulating experience, high sensation seekers choose different jobs. On the Kuder Occupational Interest Survey, high SSS scores correlated positively with scientific interests and negatively with clerical interests. High-scoring men showed interest on the Strong Interest Inventory in helping professions such as psychologist, physician, psychiatrist, social worker and minister, and low interest in business jobs such as accountant, purchasing agent and banker. High-scoring women showed high interest in law and low interest in elementary school teaching. In helping professions, both sexes preferred risky, cutting-edge work such as crisis intervention or paramedic duty. In low-level, unstimulating jobs they perform poorly.

Attitudes. High sensation seekers are more liberal in politics and religion, more likely to be atheistic, and more permissive about sex for themselves and others. They are higher in tolerance for ambiguity and lower in authoritarianism. Low sensation seekers attend church often, score high on authoritarianism (rigid opinions and prejudice) and have low tolerance for ambiguity, seeing ambiguous situations as threats rather than challenges.

practice.q: Explain how learned helplessness can develop in childhood.
practice.answer:
Seligman held that although helplessness can occur at any age, infants and young children are especially vulnerable, and early helplessness predisposes a person to a pessimistic explanatory style.

Infants start life totally helpless. As they mature, crying, crawling, walking and speaking give them growing control, and also chances of failure. When an infant responds, the response may change the environment (food, a toy, a hug) or have no effect. Infants form primitive associations between responses and outcomes. If responses do not lead to successful outcomes, they learn that those responses do not work and may generalise this to all responses, producing a general sense of having no control. A high correlation between responses and outcomes gives positive feedback and a sense of mastery.

A consistent explanatory style forms by about age 8 and is strongly affected by parents: pessimistic parents tend to have pessimistic children. Indian studies show that more parental education predicts more optimistic children, and adolescent studies show genetic as well as learned influences. Later in childhood, bullying, harsh schools, peer conflict, being treated as less able, race, poverty and low family support can produce helplessness or pessimism. The chapter summary names maternal deprivation and an environment with little stimulation and feedback as major causes.

practice.q: Describe Seligman's three types of happiness. Which corresponds most closely to Maslow's self-actualization? How does flourishing differ from subjective well-being?
practice.answer:
Three types. Seligman distinguished (1) the pleasant life, full of positive emotion such as satisfaction, job contentment, serenity and optimism; (2) the engaged life, marked by involvement, purpose, commitment and absorption in work, where time passes quickly and the sense of self is lost; and (3) the meaningful life, in which a person uses talents, abilities and strengths to belong to or serve something larger than the self, such as a religion, organisation or ideal. His research shows that pursuing meaning and engagement correlates more strongly with happiness than pursuing pleasure.

Maslow. The meaningful life corresponds most closely to self-actualization, since both involve fulfilling one's talents and potential, here in service of something beyond the self; the engaged life's absorption is also related.

Flourishing. In Flourish (2012) Seligman argued that flourishing better describes people at the top of the happiness scale, about 10 to 18 percent of the world's population, who feel happy and also excel in relationships and accomplishments. Subjective well-being concerns life satisfaction and positive emotion; flourishing treats positive emotion as only one of five pillars, adding engagement, relationships, meaning and achievement.

practice.q: Compare Seligman's positive psychology with the earlier humanistic psychology of Maslow and Rogers.
practice.answer:
Similarities. Seligman argued that psychology should deal with the best of human functioning, namely happiness, excellence and optimal human growth, rather than only problems such as helplessness and depression. This positive focus on growth and fulfilment is shared with the humanistic psychology of Maslow and Rogers. Seligman's meaningful life, using one's strengths in service of something larger than the self, resembles Maslow's self-actualization, and his concept of flourishing, which requires cultivating talents, deep relationships and positive contribution to the world, echoes humanistic ideals of full functioning.

Differences shown in this chapter. Positive psychology is presented as a large empirical research enterprise: subjective well-being is defined operationally (cognitive evaluation plus positive emotions) and measured in surveys of hundreds of thousands of people across many countries, and it is related to income, health, age, marriage, culture, personality traits and goals. It has its own journals (Journal of Happiness Studies, 2000; Journal of Positive Psychology, 2006) and produced over 10,000 articles a year by 2014. It also links happiness to inherited traits such as neuroticism and extraversion, suggesting a genetic component. Students should add detail about Maslow's and Rogers's methods from their own chapters.

practice.q: Define locus of control.
practice.answer: Locus of control is Rotter's term for a person's belief about the source of reinforcement. People with an internal locus of control believe rewards depend on their own behaviour and abilities; those with an external locus believe rewards are controlled by other people, fate or luck. It is measured with the 23-item forced-choice I-E Scale.

practice.q: What is sensation seeking?
practice.answer: Sensation seeking, studied by Zuckerman, is the need for varied, novel, complex and intense sensations and experiences, together with a willingness to take physical, social, legal and financial risks for them. It has four components (thrill and adventure seeking, experience seeking, disinhibition, boredom susceptibility) and is measured by the Sensation Seeking Scale.

practice.q: Define explanatory style.
practice.answer: Explanatory style is Seligman's term for the way we explain to ourselves our relative lack of control over the environment. An optimistic style (failures attributed to external, unstable, specific causes) prevents learned helplessness; a pessimistic style (internal, stable, global causes) spreads helplessness to all facets of life.

practice.q: What is subjective well-being?
practice.answer: Subjective well-being, or life satisfaction, is how positive psychologists describe the happy personality. It includes a cognitive evaluation of the quality of one's life experience and the possession of positive moods and emotions, so happiness has both rational and emotional aspects.

practice.q: What is meant by 'egocentric extraversion'?
practice.answer: Zuckerman's term for high sensation seekers, whose scores (especially on disinhibition) relate to Eysenck's extraversion and psychoticism. They are concerned with other people mainly as an audience or a source of stimulation and do not relate to others in a dependent or nurturing way.

practice.q: Briefly state the findings of the rat tumour study on learned helplessness.
practice.answer: Visintainer, Volpicelli and Seligman (1982) injected rats with tumour cells. 70 percent of rats given escapable shock rejected the tumour, compared with 50 percent with no shock and only 27 percent with inescapable shock, showing that helplessness impairs, and control improves, resistance to disease.

practice.q: List the four components of sensation seeking.
practice.answer: Using factor analysis Zuckerman identified: thrill and adventure seeking (dangerous, fast physical activities); experience seeking (novelty through travel, art, music, nonconformist lifestyle); disinhibition (uninhibited social behaviour, risky sex, impulsiveness); and boredom susceptibility (aversion to routine and predictable people).
