summary: The chapter takes a limited-domain approach, studying three specific facets: taking control (Rotter), taking chances (Zuckerman) and finding happiness (Seligman).

Rotter's locus of control is the belief that reinforcement depends on one's own behaviour (internal) or on other people, fate or luck (external); it is measured by the 23-item forced-choice I-E Scale and the Nowicki-Strickland scale.
Internals perform better at work, resist influence, value their skills, attend to cues, and have lower anxiety, higher self-esteem, more happiness and better mental and physical health.

Internality increases with age to a peak in middle age; gender differences vary by country; externality is more common in lower socioeconomic, some minority and immigrant groups, and collectivist cultures.

Internals adapt to change, are more satisfied at work, persist in study, resist Internet addiction, cope better with stress, recover faster from heart problems and take better care of their health, though findings on health care are not uniform.

Locus of control is learned; supportive, praising, consistent, non-authoritarian parents who encourage independence raise internals. It is strongly related to, but distinct from, Bandura's self-efficacy.

Zuckerman's sensation seeking is a largely inherited need for varied, novel, complex and intense experience, measured by the 40-item SSS, with four components: thrill and adventure seeking, experience seeking, disinhibition and boredom susceptibility.

Good (socialized, non-impulsive) sensation seeking involves thrill and adventure seeking; bad (unsocialized, impulsive) sensation seeking involves disinhibition, experience seeking, boredom susceptibility and psychoticism.
Sensation seeking is higher among the young (middle school to early 20s), men, Whites and Westerners; thrill seeking and disinhibition decline with age but experience seeking does not.

High sensation seekers take physical risks, use drugs and alcohol, drive fast, gamble, take sexual risks, have tattoos, cheat more and perform poorly in dull jobs; antisocial and adventurous risk takers score higher than pro-social ones.

High sensation seekers are egocentrically extraverted, open, conscientious, autonomous and nonconforming but not neurotic; they are modestly more intelligent and original, prefer science and helping professions, and hold liberal, permissive attitudes, while low scorers are authoritarian and intolerant of ambiguity.
Sensation seeking is about 58 percent genetic (Eysenck), but culture, parents, schools and possibly birth order shape its level and expression.

Seligman discovered learned helplessness when dogs exposed to inescapable shock stopped trying to escape; it has been shown in humans (Hiroto), through observation of helpless models, and even more strongly in humans than animals.

Helplessness harms physical health: rats with inescapable shock rejected tumours only 27 percent of the time (versus 50 and 70 percent), and their T-cells and NK cells were weakened; perceived control aids emotional adjustment.
Explanatory style is how we explain lack of control: pessimists attribute failure to internal, stable, global causes; optimists to external, unstable, specific causes.
Optimists are healthier, live longer, earn better grades, handle stress better and think more flexibly, but unrealistic optimism can lead to excess drinking, disappointment and continued gambling.

A pessimistic style turns helplessness into depression, the 'ultimate pessimism' (70 versus 30 percent depressed after failure); explanatory style forms by about age 8 and reflects parents, genes and childhood experience.
Seligman founded positive psychology in the late 1990s; subjective well-being combines a cognitive evaluation of life with positive emotions.

Money, health and attractiveness are necessary but not sufficient for happiness; marriage, social support, wealthy individualistic cultures, ethnic identity and absence of discrimination are linked to higher well-being.

Happy people are low in neuroticism and high in extraversion, agreeableness and conscientiousness, feel competent and in control, think positively, pursue meaningful goals, and tend to be more successful, healthier and longer-lived.
Seligman distinguished the pleasant, engaged and meaningful lives, and later proposed flourishing, built on positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning and achievement.
